title: From the Editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: My father-in-law built this bench and surprised me with it at Christmas when I first started gardening. I could immediately picture it nestled into a beautiful woodland garden under our big silver maple tree. So that spring, I ordered a few little perennials, gratefully accepted some hosta divisions, invested in a yew and a hydrangea at our local garden center, tucked in a couple of six-packs of impatiens for color and got a load of mulch from a local tree company. This garden definitely wasn’t the lush show I dreamed of, but it was a start.

title: From the Editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When my husband and I finally settled onto the bench to enjoy our accomplishment, we realized that we’d sited it with a perfect view of the nearby apartment building’s dumpster. Big miss. But I did learn to always think about the view from a bench as well as the view of a bench!

title: From the Editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: This piece of furniture has moved a lot over the years. It’s been refreshed a couple of times. It’s appeared in photos on these pages. Now we live in a different house and it’s sitting under a different maple tree (this time with a more carefully considered view). I’ll always find room for this classic, mostly because of who made it.

title: From the Editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: As I dig into this year’s garden, of course I’m hoping for big results. But I’m also cultivating memories. Of the people that have shared plants and advice. Of caring for it with my family. Of the excitement, disappointment and funny stories that happened there. I hope that you find all of this and more in your garden this year.

title: Reader Tips: Cart around your cucumbers
author: Joan Western, MA
content: Because her container-grown cucumber was heavy and hard to move around her balcony, Joan decided to put it on wheels: She grabbed an unused collapsible shopping cart trolley and plopped the cucumber container within. It now lives on her balcony and is easy to care for and move to chase the sun or make room for visitors.

title: Reader Tips: DIY work station
author: Mary Martin, ID
content: If you can find a used kitchen sink at the thrift store - or even have an old one of your own - you can craft an outdoor work table with Mary’s guidance.

title: Reader Tips: DIY work station
author: Mary Martin, ID
content: To begin, build a three-walled base by stacking cinder blocks in a U-shape. See in the illustration below that the lip of the sink rests on the cinder block base. Mary added a gravel drainage basin below the sink drain: She dug a hole and filled it with gravel to avoid a muddy mess. Another option is to place a bucket under the drain to catch the water so you can reuse it in the garden.

title: Reader Tips: DIY work station
author: Mary Martin, ID
content: To wash her pots and tools, she plugs the drain and fills the sink with water. When she’s finished, she lets the water drain into the gravel, where it disperses into the soil.

title: Reader Tips: DIY work station
author: Mary Martin, ID
content: You could also hook a length of hose into the faucet opening so you have a running water option.

title: Reader Tips: Bulb markers
author: Lou Emmons, IL
content: After your spring bulbs fade and the foliage disappears, it’s easy to lose track of where the bulbs are planted. To avoid digging up hidden clumps of bulbs as she plants throughout the growing season, Lou uses a few plastic landscape fabric pegs to mark the place of the bulbs in the garden bed. Because they are green, they blend in, and they’re long and sturdy enough to stay in place for years. She pushes them nearly all the way into the soil; the flat, rounded top can still be spotted but won’t be noticeable from afar.

title: Reader Tips: Pistachio shell drainage
author: Orlando Maione, NY
content: Reader Tips: Keep leftover nut shells, like pistachios, and reuse them for your containers. Fill the bottom couple of inches with the shells before topping with fresh potting mix. The shells prevent the mix from slipping through the drainage holes and causing a mess.

title: Reader Tips: Take a soak
author: Gail Wintersteiner, MA
content: Don’t give up on plants that have dried out in the nursery pot before you can plant. Gail has a trick to rehydrate them: She submerges the plant, nursery pot and all, into a larger pot or bin full of water up to or even above the crown. While the plant is submerged, you will see bubbles. This means that water is soaking into the pockets of the root ball and not just running past the roots.

title: Reader Tips: Take a soak
author: Gail Wintersteiner, MA
content: When the bubbles stop, the soil is hydrated and the plant will have better access to the moisture it needs to recuperate before being planted into its permanent home.

title: The Wild Side: Meadow fritillary
content: (Boloria bellona). Appearance: This butterfly’s bright orange wings are 1 1/2 to 2 inches wide and have irregular black markings similar to leopard spots. Three rows of dots line the outer edge of the wing. The underside of the hindwing is more mottled brown and purple-gray. Caterpillars are dark purple-gray with rows of bristled spines.

title: The Wild Side: Meadow fritillary
content: (Boloria bellona). Life cycle: Female meadow fritillaries lay single pale-yellow eggs on twigs and leaves near their host plants - violets, particularly the sweet violet (Viola sororia). The caterpillar emerges and feeds on violet flowers and leaves before forming a spiny brown chrysalis. Typically two generations occur in a year, one in late spring and the other in early fall. Caterpillars overwinter in debris before pupating and emerging in spring. These nonmigratory butterflies generally stay in the same area all year.

title: The Wild Side: Meadow fritillary
content: (Boloria bellona). Habitat: You’ll find meadow fritillary throughout southern Canada, across Midwestern and mid-Atlantic states and in New England. Within this range, it prefers sunny meadows on the edge of forests and near wetlands or a water source. If you want to attract it to your garden, you’ll need to have a collection of violets nearby for the caterpillars to munch on.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: As winter comes to an end and spring starts to gift us with the warmth of the sun, garden centers and nurseries begin to put out the first flowers of the year. This early enthusiasm inevitably results in a cart filled with plants that you can’t resist, even if you don’t really have room for them. No matter, containers are always an option!

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Place Your Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Place Your Containers. Plant up a few spring containers and a bare patio or terrace is suddenly filled with color. Your balcony becomes a bright spot in the apartment complex and neighbors are asking where those plants came from. Grouping containers together provides an even bigger show that draws attention to the entry, or you can use bright blooms to dress up a tabletop on the deck. Spring containers are just the beginning of all the ways you can express yourself this growing season.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Place Your Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Place Your Containers. Once they fade, you can get creative again by swapping plants out for a whole new look in summer and fall.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Place Your Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Place Your Containers. In the meantime, get inspired by the containers here and maybe you’ll have to make another trip to the garden center!

author: Marisa Reyes

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Bold Spring Color
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Bold Spring Color. This combination is perfect on a patio or next to your front entry because its bold colors make a statement that lasts for weeks. Plus you can enjoy the light, sweet scent of the pansy and nemesia as you walk by.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Bold Spring Color
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Bold Spring Color. Cool spring temperatures help these flowers last, but eventually you’ll need to deadhead. Pinch or snip pansy, nemesia and marguerite daisy stems back to a leaf joint to encourage more blooms. The daffodil only blooms once. So when it’s done you can pull the bulbs if you’d like to avoid unsightly yellowing bulb foliage as it ripens in the container. The red osier dogwood stems cut from the garden provide height, color and texture even when the flowers are fading.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Bold Spring Color
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Bold Spring Color. Once the weather starts getting warmer, stems can get leggy and flowering slows. This is a good time to replace cool-weather plants, such as the pansy and nemesia. You can leave the gaura and marguerite daisy in place to add height and interest to late-season combos.

title: Plant Profile: Marguerite daisy
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Argyranthemum) Grandaisy® Red Improved. Tender perennial; red flowers in spring; full sun to part shade; 18 to 24 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Plant Profile: Gaura
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Gaura lindheimeri) Belleza® Dark Pink. Perennial; star-shaped dark pink flowers in spring to fall; full sun to part shade; 18 in. tall, 16 to 20 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: Plant Profile: Pansy
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Viola x wittrockiana) Spring Matrix™ Scarlet. Perennial; scarlet red blooms with a yellow center in early to late spring and fall; full sun to part shade; 8 to 10 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Plant Profile: Nemesia Sunsatia Blood Orange
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Nemesia) Sunsatia® Blood Orange™. Tender perennial; orange, red and yellow blooms from early spring to frost; full sun to part shade; 10 to 14 in. tall, 12 to 16 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Plant Profile: Nemesia Nesia Sunshine
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Nemesia) Nesia™ Sunshine. Tender perennial; buttery yellow flowers with purple centers bloom in early spring to late summer; full sun to part shade; 10 to 14 in. tall, 10 to 12 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 10.

title: Plant Profile: Miniature daffodil
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Narcissus hybrid). Bulb; yellow flowers in spring; full sun to part shade; 4 to 24 in. tall, 3 to 12 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Accent with Cut Stems
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Accent with Cut Stems. Young dogwood stems that are less than 3 years old have the most color. To make sure you have plenty of stems to cut for spring containers, cut a third of the oldest stems (they’re usually thicker and grayer) back to the ground each year in early spring.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Bold Spring Color
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Full-page photo of the Bold Spring Color container with red marguerite daisies, red dogwood stems, scarlet pansies, orange and yellow nemesia, miniature daffodils, and yellow-green flowers in a copper-colored pot.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Petite Pastel Palette
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Petite Pastel Palette. This sweet little cool-season planter makes the perfect addition to a tabletop. You can still see your conversation partner across the table because the pint-sized plants won’t grow too tall in spring. As warmer weather approaches, the kale, sweet alyssum and viola will start to outgrow this 12-inch pot. But you can plant them in the border to enjoy blooms again later in fall, or just toss them on the compost pile.

title: Plant Profile: Ornamental kale
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Brassica oleracea) ‘Dynasty Red’. Tender perennial; rosettes of blue-green leaves with a deep red center; full sun to part shade; 12 to 18 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11.

title: Plant Profile: English daisy
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Bellis perennis) ‘Pomponette Mix’. Perennial; pink or white blooms in spring to early summer; full sun to part shade; 4 to 6 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Plant Profile: Lewisia
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Lewisia cotyledon) ‘Elise Mix’. Perennial; pink, rose, salmon or purple flowers bloom from spring to fall; full sun to part shade; 6 to 8 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Plant Profile: Sweet alyssum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Lobularia maritima) ‘Snow Crystals’. Tender perennial; clusters of fragrant white flowers from early spring to frost; full sun to part shade; 6 to 10 in. tall, 12 to 14 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: Plant Profile: Viola
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Viola cornuta) Sorbet® XP Beaconsfield. Perennial; white and purple blooms with yellow centers bloom in early spring and again until frost; full sun to part shade; 6 to 8 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers: Four-Season Structure
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Get a Head Start with Spring Containers - Four-Season Structure. Adding evergreens, such as boxwood, to a container is a great way to get structure in every season. ‘Green Velvet’ is tolerant of pruning and can be shaped however you like. Hold off on pruning until all danger of frost has passed in spring to avoid damaging tender new shoots. When you’re growing shrubs in containers, get one that’s as large as possible (these are 24 inches in diameter) so there’s plenty of room for potting mix to hold moisture and help insulate the roots. To get boxwoods through winter in zone 5, spray an antitranspirant to help prevent moisture loss and burned foliage, and water occasionally if temps are above freezing.

title: Plant Profile: Boxwood
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Buxus) ‘Green Velvet’. Shrub; glossy green leaves all year; full sun to part shade; 2 to 4 ft. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Plant Profile: Pansy
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Viola x wittrockiana). Perennial; blue and white bicolored flowers in early spring to frost; full sun to part shade; 6 to 8 in. tall, 8 to 12 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Plant Profile: Lobelia
author: Marisa Reyes
content: (Lobelia erinus). Tender perennial; white flowers in spring to fall; full sun to part shade; 6 to 14 in. tall, 6 to 16 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: Smart Plant Swaps
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When you fall in love with a plant at the garden center, you might not realize the challenges it may face at home. How many times have you had to fight back stems from a too-large plant that’s eating your sidewalk, pull unwanted seedlings, watch deer eat stems to the ground or water, water, water a gasping plant? At some point, enough is enough and the plant has to go. That’s not to say that it isn’t a perfectly good plant - it’s just that there might be better alternatives in certain situations. So you can move the offender to a new place in the garden better suited to its characteristics, give it to a friend or even just toss it on the compost pile, but that still leaves a hole to fill. The good news is that there are usually other plant options, whether you need something that’s smaller, more drought-tolerant or less aggressive. Let’s take a look at some smart swaps.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Cutting zinnia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Zinnia elegans). Zinnias for cutting are great for bouquets and they bloom nonstop. But sometimes you want a smaller plant that brings long-lasting color to the front of the border.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Bedding zinnia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Zinnia hybrids). For long-lasting color on a pint-sized plant, bedding zinnias are just the ticket. This group of hybrids has even more, though smaller, blooms than their taller cousins, cutting zinnias. They’re also quite disease resistant, so powdery mildew won’t usually crop up like it does with the taller cutting types. Besides that, bedding zinnias are self cleaning - new growth covers over the old - so no deadheading is needed!

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Bedding zinnia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Zinnia hybrids). There are lots of varieties to choose from in a range of sizes and colors. Double Zahara™ Salmon at right grows 16 to 20 inches tall and wide, while the easy-to-find Profusion series is 12 to 18 inches tall and wide. If you’re looking for an even smaller zinnia, check out the new Belize series, which grows just 8 inches tall and 12 inches wide.

title: Plant Profile: Bedding zinnia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Zinnia hybrids). Annual; blooms are single or double in every color but blue from late spring to frost; light: full sun; soil: average, well-drained; size: look for dwarf varieties that grow 6 to 20 in. tall, 10 to 24 in. wide; source: local garden centers.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Zinnias
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Illustrated smart-swap diagram comparing tall cutting zinnias with a smaller mounded bedding zinnia plant for front-of-border color.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Bedding zinnia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Full-page photo of Double Zahara Salmon bedding zinnia, showing masses of compact salmon-pink double blooms along a stone path.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Solomon's seal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Polygonatum spp. and hybrids). At up to 4 feet tall with an arching habit, Solomon’s seal takes up a lot of room and can block the view of other plants in the garden.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Dwarf Solomon's seal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Polygonatum humile). This little perennial is amazingly cute! But even better, it’s one tough customer. Dwarf Solomon’s seal grows well in wet garden soil but tolerates drought, performs beautifully even in full shade and doesn’t have any serious insect or disease problems or need a lot of maintenance to look fantastic.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Dwarf Solomon's seal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Polygonatum humile). Plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form colonies, making it an attractive ground cover for shade. Tubular white 3/4-inch flowers emerge in spring and are followed by blue-black fruits - both are easy to see on those short upright stems. Alternate pairs of ovate leaves provide rich texture that contrasts well with broader foliage of hosta (Hosta hybrids) or coral bells (Heuchera hybrids).

title: Plant Profile: Dwarf Solomon's seal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Polygonatum humile). Perennial; blooms: tubular white blooms with a green edge from late spring to early summer; light: part to full shade; soil: moist, well-drained; size: 6 to 9 in. tall, spreading; cold hardy: USDA zones 4 to 8; source: Avant Gardens, 508-998-8819, avantgardensne.com.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Dwarf Solomon's seal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Photo of dwarf Solomon’s seal forming a low, spreading colony with white tubular flowers around the base of a tree in shade.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Russian sage
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Perovskia atriplicifolia). These large plants tend to flop and lean later in the season and can be a real pain to stake.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Dwarf Russian sage
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Perovskia atriplicifolia). If you don’t have room for a huge Russian sage that can reach 5 feet tall and 4 feet wide, you don’t have to miss out on growing this heat-, drought-, deer- and rabbit-resistant plant. There are a lot of new dwarf varieties with the same lavender-blue blooms that last for weeks, thanks in part to the colorful bracts that hang on after true flowers fall off. ‘Denim ’n Lace’ in the photo at left grows 32 inches tall and has a fuller look than some because the flowers are so closely spaced. It has strong upright stems that won’t flop open as the plant ages, as some of the larger varieties’ foliage does. ‘Little Spire’ is a bit smaller, growing just 24 inches tall.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Dwarf Russian sage
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Perovskia atriplicifolia). Maintenance is simple: Just cut stems back to the crown in late winter to early spring to make way for new growth.

title: Plant Profile: Dwarf Russian sage
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Perovskia atriplicifolia). Perennial; blooms: long spikes lined with lavender-blue flowers from midsummer to fall; light: full sun; soil: well-drained; size: look for dwarf varieties that grow 28 to 32 in. tall, 34 to 38 in. wide; cold hardy: USDA zones 4 to 9; source: local garden centers.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Dwarf Russian sage
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Photo of ‘Denim ’n Lace’ Russian sage with upright lavender-blue flower spikes planted in front of pink hibiscus and burgundy foliage.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Love-in-a-mist
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Nigella damascena). The flowers are pretty, but this annual can reseed vigorously and become a nuisance.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Pincushion flower
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Scabiosa spp. and hybrids). When you want a blue flower that you don’t have to worry about reseeding in your beds, choose pincushion flower. This perennial is easy to care for, blooms for weeks, stems can be cut for summer bouquets and butterflies love it! ‘Butterfly Blue’ is well known for its profusion of 2-inch blooms that ensure plenty of fluttering visitors. Plants grow 12 to 18 inches tall and wide. ‘Blue Note’ at right is smaller, at 8 to 10 inches tall and wide. For pink flowers, grow 12- to 18-inch-tall ‘Pink Mist.’

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Pincushion flower
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Scabiosa spp. and hybrids). Deadheading will help encourage new blooms to form more quickly on your pincushion flower. To do this, follow the long stem back to the mound of foliage and cut it off below the leaves.

title: Plant Profile: Pincushion flower
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Scabiosa spp. and hybrids). Perennial; blooms: lavender-blue, pink or white blooms with a dome-shaped center and frilly petals from early summer to fall; light: full sun to part shade; soil: well-drained; size: 4 to 36 in. tall, 4 to 18 in. wide; cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 10; source: local garden centers.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Pincushion flower
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Photo of ‘Blue Note’ pincushion flower with lavender-blue frilly blooms and rounded centers in a close-up planting.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Morning glory
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Ipomoea purpurea). Whew! Talk about reseeding. Plant morning glory once and seedlings will come back for years.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: 'Jackmanii' clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Clematis spp. and hybrids). Clematis brings loads of color to your trellis or arbor without taking over the structure. ‘Jackmanii’ is a classic variety that produces lots of gorgeous 5- to 7-inch deep-purple blooms every summer and grows 7 to 10 feet tall. For a slightly larger plant, try 10- to 12-foot-tall ‘Lady Betty Balfour,’ which also has deep purple blooms. If pink if your preference, ‘Comtesse de Bouchaud’ will fit the bill.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: 'Jackmanii' clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Clematis spp. and hybrids). When you’re planting, go deep. Position the young clematis so its first two leaf nodes are below the soil. This encourages more stems to grow, creating a bushier plant with even more blooms. A couple inches of organic mulch helps plants grow happily by keeping soil moisture and temperatures cool. Pruning is simple: In late winter to early spring, cut all of last year’s growth to within a foot of the ground.

title: Plant Profile: 'Jackmanii' clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Clematis spp. and hybrids). Woody vine; blooms: purple flowers in early to late summer; light: full sun to part shade; soil: evenly moist, well-drained; size: 7 to 10 ft. tall, spreading; cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 9; source: Brushwood Nursery, brushwoodnursery.com.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Morning glory
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Inset photo of blue and pink morning glory flowers used as an example of a reseeding plant.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: 'Jackmanii' clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Large photo of ‘Jackmanii’ clematis with deep-purple flowers scrambling over stonework.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Hosta
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Hosta spp. and hybrids). If you have visiting deer, you know how much they love hostas - those leaves don’t stand a chance.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Pulmonaria
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Pulmonaria spp. and hybrids). The fuzzy foliage of pulmonaria makes it less than appealing for deer, and even better, it thrives in a range of conditions, including dry shade. In fact, too much water causes pulmonaria to rot.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Pulmonaria
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Pulmonaria spp. and hybrids). Flowers arrive on upright stems with small leaves in early spring before the mound of larger foliage takes off. Bell-shaped blooms are often a mix of pink, purple and blue, such as those of ‘Mrs. Moon’ or ‘Victorian Brooch.’ But there are exceptions. ‘Trevi Fountain’ at right has cobalt-blue flowers, ‘Sissinghurst White’ has white ones and ‘Raspberry Splash’ blooms in pink. As the flowers fade, their stems lean toward the ground. You can cut them off as close to the base of the plant as possible to tidy up the plant. But it’s not a problem if you forget. The speckled leaves will still take off and form an attractive mound.

title: Plant Profile: Pulmonaria
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Pulmonaria spp. and hybrids). Perennial; blooms: bell-shaped pink, purple, blue or white blooms in early spring; light: part to full shade; soil: average, well-drained; size: 6 to 18 in. tall, 10 to 40 in. wide; cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 9; source: local garden centers.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Lilyturf
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Liriope spicata). Lilyturf is a good-looking plant for borders or containers, but deer find it pretty tasty, and some of the decorative varieties aren’t very cold hardy.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Appalachian sedge
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Carex appalachica). Often overlooked and under appreciated, this cool-season native grass has a tidy clumping habit and won’t spread aggressively. The long, slender stems grow up and then drape over, creating a wavy texture that’s great for edging your border or as a low-maintenance lawn alternative. Wondering what in the world will grow under a shallow-rooted maple (Acer spp. and hybrids) or pine (Pinus spp.) tree? This sedge is up to the challenge.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Appalachian sedge
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Carex appalachica). Appalachian sedge is evergreen in mild winter areas. But even so, you’ll want to mow it high or cut the foliage back to the ground in late winter to early spring just like in colder climates to tidy plants up.

title: Plant Profile: Appalachian sedge
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Carex appalachica). Perennial; blooms: inconspicuous sporadic blooms in spring; light: full sun to part shade; soil: well-drained; size: 6 to 12 in. tall, 8 to 18 in. wide; cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8; source: High Country Gardens, 800-925-9387, highcountrygardens.com.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Astilbe
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Astilbe spp. and hybrids). Those lovely plumes will last for weeks, but leaves get crispy and plants don’t grow or flower as well without enough water.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Smooth penstemon
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Penstemon digitalis). When you want lots of white blooms but need a plant that isn’t thirsty, North American native smooth penstemon is a great alternative. Plus, it tolerates clay soil, pollinators love it and deer tend to pass it by.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Smooth penstemon
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Penstemon digitalis). There are plenty of cultivars to choose from and many have interesting foliage. ‘Husker Red’ at right is an old favorite with loads of white flowers and burgundy spring foliage that matures to dark green by summer. Plants grow 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide. ‘Mystica’ has clusters of white flowers and puts on quite the foliage show with leaves that start out green in spring, mature to deep purple by summer and then turn red in fall. Plants grow 28 to 32 inches tall in zones 4 to 8.

title: Plant Profile: Smooth penstemon
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Penstemon digitalis). Perennial; blooms: tubular lavender, pink or white blooms from late spring to summer; light: full sun; soil: well-drained; size: 2 to 3 ft. tall, 1 to 3 ft. wide; cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8; source: local garden centers.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: Cardinal flower
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Lobelia cardinalis). It’s easy to love this perennial’s vibrant red flower spikes in summer. But if you have to water frequently to keep it going, it might be time to try something else.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: 'Asian Garden' celosia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Celosia argentea spicata). ‘Asian Garden’ celosia provides long-lasting color and head-turning drama for those mid- to back-of-the-border spots in the garden that are hard to water. At 40 inches tall, this variety is taller than many of its cousins, getting color closer to eye level. There are plenty of flowers to add to your summer bouquets, so you can cut freely without sacrificing any color in the garden. Cut late-season stems and hang them to dry in a cool, dry spot for a few weeks so you can enjoy the colorful blooms even in winter.

title: Smart Plant Swaps: 'Asian Garden' celosia
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: (Celosia argentea spicata). Because it takes 12 to 14 weeks for ‘Asian Garden’ celosia to bloom, it’s a good idea to start the seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the average last frost date for your area. Plants can be planted outdoors when nighttime temperatures are regularly 55 degrees F or above.

title: Attract More Birds to Your Yard This Spring!
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds to Your Yard This Spring! Placing nesting boxes around your garden is a great way to encourage feathery friends to start a family there. With more birds in the yard, you’ll enjoy the benefits of these little garden helpers as they eat unwanted insects, munch on pesky weed seeds and help pollinate your flowers. Plus, watching them build their nests and raise chicks is great entertainment!

title: Attract More Birds to Your Yard This Spring!
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds to Your Yard This Spring! I spoke with Robyn Bailey, NestWatch Project Leader at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in New York, about how you can make your birdhouses safe and welcoming nesting boxes for the birds you want to host. She reminded me that different species of birds prefer different house styles and locations and shared a few things to keep in mind as you decide what works best.

title: Attract More Birds: Which Birds Will Visit?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Which birds will visit? Common North American backyard birds include American kestrel, barn swallow, chickadees, flycatchers, mourning dove, northern flicker, nuthatches, owls, purple martin, robin, tufted titmouse, warblers and wrens.

title: Attract More Birds: Housekeeping Help
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - Housekeeping Help. Clean out nesting boxes once a year before breeding season starts (by February in the South and mid-March in the North) or at the end of summer when it’s over. Since bird nests are susceptible to parasites and diseases, it’s a good idea to wear gloves and toss old nests and debris in the garbage rather than the compost. Once you’ve cleared a box, scrub it with a mixture of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water and give it a good rinse.

title: Attract More Birds: Housekeeping Help
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - Housekeeping Help. The type of birds who are visiting and nesting in your yard will determine whether or not you should add any nest materials. Some birds, such as American kestrel, northern flicker, chickadees and owls, appreciate a layer of wood shavings in the bottom of the box, but most birds prefer to find their own nest materials.

title: Attract More Birds: To Paint or Not to Paint?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - To Paint or Not to Paint? It’s not necessary. For protection from predators, a nesting box that blends into its surroundings is usually best. But painting the outside of a box white to reflect the sun helps control temperatures. If you do want to paint, use nontoxic acrylic or latex paint or wood stain on the exterior and leave the inside unfinished.

title: Attract More Birds to Your Yard This Spring!
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Illustrations of colorful birds, leaves and sun around a Garden Gate article on attracting more birds with safe nesting boxes.

title: Attract More Birds: Robyn Bailey
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Portrait of Robyn Bailey, NestWatch Project Leader at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, included with nesting-box advice.

title: Attract More Birds: Nesting Box Types
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - Nesting Box Types. House wrens prefer a round 1-inch hole. Purple martins nest in colonies but prefer houses that are 60 feet away from nearby buildings. Mount a purple martin house on a pole 10 to 15 feet tall. American robins utilize nesting shelves mounted in a sheltered spot. Mourning doves nest in the open - make a basket of hardware cloth and place it in a forked branch or on top of an arbor.

title: Attract More Birds: What Makes a Good Nesting Box?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - What Makes a Good Nesting Box? First, for most houses, a sloped roof with a 2- to 4-inch overhang will keep the inside dry and predators away by limiting their reach to the entrance hole. Second, add some drainage holes to the floor of the nesting box in case it does get wet inside. Third, 3/4-inch-thick walls and a 5/8-inch hole on each of the side walls near the top of the box are important for ventilation and keeping temperatures regulated. Finally, skip the perch outside the entrance - it’s just an invitation for predators.

title: Attract More Birds: What Makes a Good Nesting Box?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - What Makes a Good Nesting Box? The style of the house and the size of the entrance hole and house will determine which type of bird might take up residence. Check out a sampling of nesting box types above. If invasive house sparrows are a problem in your yard, only provide houses with the smallest entrance holes since these birds will move into anything 1 1/4 inch in diameter and larger.

title: Attract More Birds: Right Bird, Right House
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Right Bird, Right House. Learn all the information you need to know about each bird’s specific birdhouse requirements and more (including how to predator-proof). Visit nestwatch.org and click the “learn” tab.

title: Attract More Birds: Keep Spacing & Height in Mind
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - Keep Spacing & Height in Mind. Many birds prefer to nest 20 feet or more from another bird of the same species, but don’t seem to mind if other species nest nearby, as long as they aren’t predatory, such as owls.

title: Attract More Birds: Keep Spacing & Height in Mind
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - Keep Spacing & Height in Mind. Songbirds like chickadees and wrens are happy to have their nesting boxes at a convenient height for humans to reach for cleaning and mounting. However, some birds prefer a height that’s a little more difficult to access: Owls and wood ducks prefer to nest 10 to 30 feet above ground.

title: Attract More Birds: Predator Guard
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Did you know? Cornell’s research has shown that a predator guard placed on the pole or tree can improve the odds of a nest succeeding by 7%.

title: Attract More Birds: Where Not to Put a Nesting Box
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Attract More Birds - Where Not to Put a Nesting Box. Skip these spots when you’re looking for real estate for your feathered friends: Next to bird feeders and bird baths. This makes them an easy target for predators, such as cats and raccoons, which frequent these spots. High-traffic areas close to the mailbox or the front door. Even though some birds, such as Carolina wren, happily build nests in those spots, others, such as tufted titmouse, are shy and prefer to be farther away from people. Near drainpipes, an overhang or gutters. They’re too easy for predators to climb.

author: Marisa Reyes
content: Illustrated diagram of bird-specific nesting options, including a wren box with a 1-inch hole, a purple martin colony house on a 10- to 15-foot pole, a robin nesting shelf, and a mourning dove hardware-cloth basket.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Japanese Iris
content: (Iris ensata). The last iris of the season to bloom, Japanese iris can also have the largest flowers: Some are up to 10 inches in diameter. And what flowers they are! The unusual and orchidlike blossoms invite a closer inspection of their intricate design.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Japanese Iris
content: Japanese irises like moist, acid soil, which makes them ideal along the edge of natural water features, near downspouts or in rain gardens. Or plant them in a border with other moisture-loving perennials, such as ligularia (Ligularia dentata) or Japanese anemone (Anemone x hybrida), where their spiky foliage will contrast with rounded leaves and mounded habits.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Japanese Iris
content: For the best blooms and healthiest foliage, plant Japanese iris in full sun, but plants will tolerate part shade as well. Provide plants 2 or more inches of water per week, especially in spring leading up to the early summer bloom time. Though they can be submerged in water up to the crown, it’s better to plant close to the water where it is moist but not saturated. In winter, the rhizomes can rot in cold, wet soil or standing water. Divide plants every 2 to 3 years to maintain robust growth. Japanese iris is hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Japanese Iris Facts
content: Japanese iris facts: Blooms are flatter than those of other irises, with yellow markings and a central rib highlighting where a beard would be on many other types of irises. Leaves are sword-shaped with a prominent midrib, often relax and curve down some at the tips. Habit is upright fans of leaves growing 24 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide. Roots are small rhizomes, appearing more like thickened roots. Japanese iris rhizomes grow and multiply upward, not out horizontally like those of bearded iris. Sources: Cascadia Iris Gardens, cascadianirisgardens.com; Ensata Gardens, ensata.com; Mt. Pleasant Iris Farm, mtpleasantiris.com.

title: Plant Profile: 'Flamingo Waltz' Japanese iris
content: ‘Flamingo Waltz’ Japanese iris. Six soft-pink falls, or lower petals, create the 7- to 8-inch-wide open blossom in midsummer. It grows 36 inches tall in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Plant Profile: 'Frosted Intrigue' Japanese iris
content: ‘Frosted Intrigue’ Japanese iris. Midsummer blooms in shades of dark blue with violet and a touch of white. Grows 36 inches tall in USDA zones 5 to 10.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Japanese Iris
content: Botanical illustration of Japanese iris showing flatter blooms, sword-shaped leaves, upright fans, small rhizome-like roots, and callouts for bloom, leaf, habit, and root traits.

title: Japanese Iris Cultivars
content: Two cultivar photos for Japanese iris: soft-pink ‘Flamingo Waltz’ and dark blue-violet ‘Frosted Intrigue’ with a white and yellow center.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Dutch Iris
content: (Iris x hollandica). Unlike Japanese iris, spring-blooming Dutch iris is grown from a bulb and goes dormant in the summer, which might seem atypical for an iris. But the flowers are a traditional iris form and come in a multitude of solid or bicolor shades.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Dutch Iris
content: Easy to naturalize in lawns or woodland beds, Dutch iris looks great planted in drifts or groups. Or use it in a spring container, then pull the bulbs out after foliage yellows and plant in the garden later in the fall to enjoy again the following year.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Dutch Iris
content: Plant Dutch iris bulbs in fall in USDA zones 5 to 9. They like full sun to part shade with even moisture until they bloom. Once flowers are spent, let the foliage die down. Dormant bulbs prefer dry soil or they may rot. Every 3 to 4 years, if you notice your Dutch iris isn’t flowering as much, mark the clump so you can find and dig the bulbs in fall. Brush the soil off, separate the bulbs and replant them. Some gardeners simply grow Dutch iris as a spring annual and compost the plants after the blooms fade.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Dutch Iris Facts
content: Dutch iris facts: Blooms are beardless flowers with three upright petals, called “standards,” above three falling petals, known as “falls,” blooming in late spring to early summer. Leaves are grassy and fade away after flowers are spent. Habit is upright, slender plants growing in clumps and reaching 20 to 24 inches tall. Roots are teardrop-shaped bulbs that store energy for the next year. Irises used in florist bouquets are usually Dutch irises; blooms can last 5 to 7 days in a vase. Sources: American Meadows, americanmeadows.com; John Scheepers, johnscheepers.com.

title: Plant Profile: 'Oriental Beauty' Dutch iris
content: ‘Oriental Beauty’ Dutch iris. Pastel blue upright standards crown pale yellow falls in early summer. Plants grow 20 to 24 inches tall in USDA zones 5 to 10.

title: Plant Profile: 'Eye of the Tiger' Dutch iris
content: ‘Eye of the Tiger’ Dutch iris. Unique color combination of purple standards atop maroon falls with yellow accents. Grows in USDA zones 5 to 10 and can reach 18 to 24 inches tall.

title: Which Iris Is Right for You?: Dutch Iris
content: Botanical illustration of Dutch iris showing standards, beard, falls, grassy leaves, teardrop-shaped bulb roots, and bloom, leaf, habit, and root callouts.

title: Dutch Iris Cultivars
content: Two cultivar photos for Dutch iris: pastel blue and pale yellow ‘Oriental Beauty’ and purple, maroon, and yellow ‘Eye of the Tiger’.

title: Coral Bells
content: Colorful foliage and airy blossoms for any garden! Could any plant be more versatile in the garden than coral bells? Sun or shade, it’s hard to beat this easy-care perennial. With a rainbow of available foliage colors, almost anyone should be able to find one (or several!) to blend into the garden.

title: Coral Bells: All About the Foliage
content: Coral Bells - All About the Foliage. Once upon a time, coral bells were simply mounds of green foliage with thin wands of coral-pink blooms. Now you can find this perennial in shades of green, chartreuse, amber, peach, orange, red, bronze and purple. And although there are plenty of bold solid-colored varieties, such as ‘Caramel’ and ‘Black Pearl’ in the photo at right, breeders have also developed foliage with intricate vein patterns and lacy or metallic-looking overlays, as you can see on ‘Green Spice.’ All of this exciting variety makes a plant geek like me want one of each kind.

title: Coral Bells: Light and Airy Blooms
content: Coral Bells - Light and Airy Blooms. Flowers are not usually as showy as the foliage, but the spikes of dainty blossoms serve to accent the eye-catching leaves without stealing their thunder. The tiny bell-shaped blooms dangling from tall spires can be red, pink, green, coral or white, and attract hummingbirds and other pollinators to the garden. While coral bells breeding programs have mostly concentrated on unique foliage, Chuck Pavlich from Terra Nova Nurseries, a company that’s lead the way on introducing new coral bells varieties, tells us to watch for showier blossoms in the future. And with good reason: The blooms make super cut flowers—and the foliage holds up like a champ in bouquets, too.

title: Coral Bells: Native Roots
content: Coral Bells - Native Roots. Coral bells species are native to North America, growing in a variety of climates, from moist, shady woodlands to dry, sunny regions. That’s what makes new hybrids of these species so adaptable to every garden. Hybrids with Southern native Heuchera villosa, such as ‘Fire Alarm,’ in the parentage will have increased heat and drought tolerance, while the Northern Exposure™ series bred from Northern native H. richardsonii are more cold-tolerant. Keep reading to learn how to use all of these exciting plants in your garden.

title: Plant Profile: Coral Bells
content: Heuchera spp. and hybrids. Perennial. Blooms: Tiny, bell-shaped flowers in shades of red, pink, green, coral or white in late spring to fall. Light: Full sun to part shade. Soil: Moist, well-drained. Pests: None serious. Size: 6 to 24 in. tall (up to 36 in. in bloom), 10 to 36 in. wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Coral Bells
content: Plant portrait of a coral bells cultivar with minty green foliage and airy pink flower spikes, illustrating the article’s colorful foliage and bloom habit.

title: Coral Bells
content: Garden border photo showing coral bells foliage and flower spikes around a tree and path, with cultivars labeled ‘Caramel,’ ‘Black Pearl,’ and ‘Green Spice.’

title: Designing with Coral Bells
content: Once you finally choose which beautiful coral bells to buy, the next trick is to decide where to plant it! Fortunately, that’s easy, since they can perform any number of roles in the garden.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Front and Center
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Front and Center. Low-growing, colorful foliage makes coral bells ideal to grow along a path or the edge of the garden to soften the lines between the bed and a walkway or lawn. You won’t have to worry about the plants flopping over into the path, as they’ll stay put in a neat row. Coral bells’ full, mounded habit makes them perfect to tuck under larger perennials or shrubs that suffer from “bare legs,” such as lilies, peonies or inkberry, to fill in the empty space between the exposed stems and the ground.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: 'Paris'
content: Designing with Coral Bells - ‘Paris.’ Look for cultivars that rebloom, such as petite ‘Paris,’ for a long-lasting front-of-the-border show that won’t quit. Growing 7 inches tall and 14 inches wide, ‘Paris’ continually flowers from early summer to frost in USDA zones 4 to 9. Its rose-colored flowers stand 14 inches tall, floating above minty green leaves with a white overlay.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Attention Getters
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Attention Getters. See how a chartreuse coral bells plant warms and brightens the border in photo 1 below? Foliage in shades of lime, yellow, peach or even silver provide a welcome light in a shady spot. Add a bit more color with the red-veined, yellow-green leaves of ‘Electric Lime’ for an interesting focal point. Conversely, a dark-colored coral bells, such as near-black ‘Obsidian,’ tends to recede in a shady location, looking like a hole or gap in the bed from a distance. Instead, plant red, orange and purple coral bells in the sun, where they’ll look most vibrant, and eye-catching.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Amassed and Amazing
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Amassed and Amazing. One coral bells plant is a focal point. A cluster of three or five can be the backbone of a bed. But a mass planting is a sight to behold. Just look at the sea of coral bells highlighting the tree peony at right in photo 2. Grown as a ground cover, large drifts of coral bells can provide low-maintenance color all season, and their tight habit has good weed-suppressing qualities. Taller varieties, like 12-inch-tall ‘Palace Purple,’ fill in a roomy space with ease. For a mass planting, plant the coral bells half the mature width apart so they overlap and grow together quickly.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Botanical Names
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Botanical Names. Blue fescue: Festuca glauca. Cape daisy: Osteospermum hybrid. Inkberry: Ilex glabra. Lily: Lilium spp. and hybrids. Rodgersia: Rodgersia pinnata. Sedge: Carex spp. and hybrids. Tree peony: Paeonia hybrid.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Lighten Up
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Lighten up. The bright color of ‘Lemon Love’ coral bells calls attention to its round-leaved, mounded shape. It gives the eye a solid place to rest when nestled among soft, draping forms of ferns or sedges in a shady spot.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Lighten Up
content: Shade-garden photo of bright chartreuse ‘Lemon Love’ coral bells used as a mounded focal point among ferns and sedges.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: A Mass of Color
content: Designing with Coral Bells - A mass of color. Dark ‘Chocolate Ruffles’ coral bells sets the stage for ‘Hephestos’ tree peony, but keeps its glorious, rich color long after the peony blooms are gone. Creamy white flowers also appear in late spring to early summer. At 12 to 14 inches tall, it does a good job of covering the peony’s bare legs.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Contained Excitement
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Contained Excitement. Coral bells are the perfect colorful foliage filler for a container too. Their polite mound provides form and texture without becoming unruly, and you’ll even get blooms for an additional pop of color. Plant with other perennials, such as the rodgersia in photo 3, add to a container of annuals, or have a single coral bells as a specimen plant in its own pot to tie the garden in with the patio containers. In zone 6 or warmer where coral bells is reliably evergreen, plants can be overwintered right in their containers. In colder zones, dig them up before a killing frost and plant them in the garden to get them through winter more reliably.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Indoors
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Indoors. Did you know you could grow coral bells as a houseplant? Terra Nova’s Chuck Pavlich says any coral bells, especially the dwarf varieties like the Little Cuties™ series, will thrive indoors in a sunny window. But note that without a cold period, they may not bloom indoors, so just enjoy the fabulous foliage color.

title: Designing with Coral Bells
content: I bet you have an idea where to plant a few coral bells in your garden now. On the next two pages, learn how to grow them.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Fire and Spice
content: Designing with Coral Bells - Fire and spice. Planted in a ring around ‘Bronze Peacock’ rodgersia and Ostica™ Bronze cape daisy, ‘Fire Alarm’ and ‘Green Spice’ coral bells provide a foundation of color. ‘Green Spice’ even turns vibrant orange in the fall.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: A Mass of Color
content: Garden photo of dark ‘Chocolate Ruffles’ coral bells planted as a dense groundcover around ‘Hephestos’ tree peony.

title: Designing with Coral Bells: Fire and Spice
content: Container planting with ‘Fire Alarm’ and ‘Green Spice’ coral bells circling ‘Bronze Peacock’ rodgersia and Ostica™ Bronze cape daisy.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells
content: These adaptable plants can grow in sun or shade, but a general rule of thumb is that darker leaf colors are more sun tolerant than light or green cultivars. Also, leaves that are coarse or a bit hairy are more heat tolerant than those with shiny or metallic-colored leaves. But in hot Southern gardens, even coral bells that like sun appreciate a couple hours of light shade in the heat of the day, or their leaves can scorch.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells: Water Wisely
content: Grow Great Coral Bells - Water Wisely. Coral bells prefer well-drained soil, and many are drought tolerant. New varieties are often rust-resistant, but to avoid this fungal disease, be sure to water at soil level early in the day to keep foliage dry.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells: Winter Care
content: Grow Great Coral Bells - Winter Care. In cold zones, coral bells are prone to heaving, meaning their shallow root system is pushed upward as soil freezes and thaws during extreme winter temperature fluctuations, leaving roots exposed to bitter cold and potential damage. Help prevent heaving by mulching in late fall with a 2- to 3-inch layer of shredded bark, compost or straw. If your plant does heave up, in late winter or very early spring, simply use your foot and gently push the crown down (it’s OK—Chuck says it won’t hurt the plant), pressing it back into the ground. Then tuck in soil or mulch around it.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells: Spring Refresh
content: Grow Great Coral Bells - Spring Refresh. Plants are evergreen where temperatures rarely dip below freezing, but leaves may appear flattened by spring, as photo 4 above shows. A bit of trimming will tidy them up. In zones 5 and colder, leaves will mostly die back in winter. As new growth emerges in spring, cut dead foliage back to within an inch of the ground and pull mulch away from the crown to prevent wet conditions that can cause root rot. Chuck recommends applying a low-nitrogen, slow-release fertilizer in early spring.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells: Divide for More
content: Grow Great Coral Bells - Divide for More. Over time, coral bells plants elongate on woody stems, collapsing in the middle and forming new crowns on side shoots that often aren’t even in the ground. Once this begins, usually every 2 to 3 years, dig up the plant and divide it. “How to Divide Coral Bells” at right shows you how.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells: Spring Cleaning
content: Grow Great Coral Bells - Spring cleaning. Where coral bells are evergreen, flattened foliage helps protect plants from occasional low temps, so no mulch is necessary. Leaves perk up in spring, and any browned or tattered leaves can be snipped back to the crown.

title: Grow Great Coral Bells: Spring Cleaning
content: Close-up photo of flattened evergreen coral bells foliage in early spring, illustrating where browned or tattered leaves can be trimmed back to the crown.

title: How to Divide Coral Bells: Step 1
content: How to Divide Coral Bells - Step 1. Dig up the plant in late fall while the ground is still warm or early spring before new growth begins. Shake or brush the soil away to reveal shoots growing off the main crown that will become divisions.

title: How to Divide Coral Bells: Step 2
content: How to Divide Coral Bells - Step 2. Break apart or use sharp pruners to cut stems and trim off old, woody roots that don’t have any new growth. Keep divisions that have a few new roots forming along the stem to replant.

title: How to Divide Coral Bells: Step 3
content: How to Divide Coral Bells - Step 3. Plant the new stem division into the soil just below the crown. Even if it doesn’t have roots to start, it will grow, just like a stem cutting would. Be sure to keep new divisions moist for a few weeks to help establish roots.

title: How to Divide Coral Bells
content: Three-photo technique sequence showing coral bells division: small shoots forming along an above-ground stem, cutting away an old crown with no new buds, and setting a new division into soil up to the base of the crown.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Save money with these easy propagation techniques. Who doesn’t love a good bargain at the garden center? I know I do! But it’s even better when you can get more plants without having to open your wallet at all. Knowing a few easy propagation techniques can increase your collection of annuals, perennials or shrubs without putting a strain on the budget.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When annuals get lanky and leggy, cutting them back helps improve the look of the plant and why not turn a few of those stems into cuttings? If a perennial isn’t flowering like it used to, it might be overcrowded. Division helps it grow more vigorously again and adds more colorful flowers to your border. Or maybe you have an heirloom shrub that you don’t want to lose—layering is a sure-fire way to keep it going and share with others.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: These propagation techniques are super simple and most of what you’ll need is probably already in the garden shed, so let’s get started!

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Stem Cuttings
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Get More Plants with Stem Cuttings. If you’ve cut a stem of your favorite coleus and plunked it in a jar of water, you’ve taken a cutting. It’s a simple and sure technique that works for other plants, such as alternanthera and purple heart, too. But you can actually skip this step and go right to potting mix to get transplant-ready cuttings like the one at left in as little as a few weeks.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Stem Cuttings
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Stem Cuttings. Before you start cutting stems you’ll want to get a few containers and some potting medium. A mix of equal parts coarse sand and peat, perlite or vermiculite is great, but premoistened potting mix works just fine for most plants and still drains well.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Stem Cuttings
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Stem Cuttings. You can grow all kinds of plants from stem cuttings, but the tender perennials that most of us grow as annuals are the most common.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: When to Cut
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - When to Cut. Cut stems any time during the growing season. Just be sure to water the parent plant the day before and harvest your cuttings early in the morning to ensure that the stems are well hydrated and in peak condition.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: How to Cut
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - How to Cut. Look for pliable new growth near the stem tip. Older woody growth found near the base of the plant isn’t as likely to root. Use pruners or scissors to cut a 2- to 6-inch-long piece just below a leaf joint and remove the lower two to three sets of leaves (1).

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Stem-Cutting Stars
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Stem-Cutting Stars. Alternanthera: Alternanthera spp. and hybrids. Basil: Ocimum basilicum. Coleus: Plectranthus scutellarioides. Cuban oregano: Plectranthus amboinicus. English ivy: Hedera helix. Iresine: Iresine herbstii. Penstemon: Penstemon spp. and hybrids. Purple heart: Tradescantia pallida ‘Purpurea’. Salvia: Salvia spp. and hybrids. Wallflower: Erysimum hybrids.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Stem Cuttings
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Photo of a small rooted stem cutting with fresh green leaves and visible roots, illustrating a transplant-ready cutting grown in potting mix.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Rooting Hormone
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Rooting Hormone. This is the time to apply rooting hormone (2) if you’re going to. It’s not essential, but it can help some plants take off more quickly. Rooting hormone is available as a powder, gel or liquid and in different strengths, depending on the type of plant you’re propagating. The weakest strength —0.1— is sufficient for stem cuttings like these. Stick the exposed leaf joints in the potting mix and firm the mix in place.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Encourage Your Cuttings
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Encourage Your Cuttings. Place the cuttings-filled container (3) under grow lights or in the indirect sunlight of a south-facing window. Keep the growing medium moist but not soggy and the temperature between 65 to 75 degrees F. Use a nursery flat with a plastic lid or create a tent with a plastic bag to provide extra humidity. You’ll know the stems have formed roots when a gentle tug meets with some resistance. This can take a few weeks or a few months, depending on the plant. Once the roots are at least an inch long, transplant the cuttings to a slightly larger container. When there are three or four new sets of leaves, they’re ready to be hardened off and planted outdoors.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Stem Cutting Callouts
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Stem cutting callouts. Pinch off the growth tip to encourage branching. Cut just below a leaf joint; this is where roots will form. The leaves that were cut off and any leftover stem pieces can be tossed. Pour a bit of rooting hormone into a separate container before using it to prevent contaminating the powder in the original vessel.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Preparing Cuban Oregano Cuttings
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Technique photo showing Cuban oregano stem cuttings prepared on a table, with callouts for pinching the growth tip, cutting below a leaf joint, and discarding removed leaves and leftover stem pieces.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Rooting Hormone
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Technique photo showing a stem cutting being inserted into potting mix after using rooting hormone from a separate container to avoid contaminating the original powder.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Cutting Flat
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Nursery flat of young cuttings labeled variegated Cuban oregano, iresine, alternanthera, and Cuban oregano.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Division
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Get More Perennials with Division. When you want more perennials, division is the fastest and simplest method. All you need is a spade or garden fork. You can divide most perennials, but those with taproots, such as butterfly weed or baptisia, don’t bounce back as reliably as those with fibrous root systems, such as garden phlox or daylily.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: When to Divide
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - When to Divide. Spring is a great time to divide. It’s cooler and there’s usually plenty of rain so plants aren’t stressed out before or after being dug. Plus, new growth is just getting started. Fall is also a good time: Temperatures are cooling down and the sun isn’t as intense, so plants can recover more easily. Be sure to allow 4 to 6 weeks before your expected first frost so plants have time to put on a few roots before the soil freezes. This will help them survive winter.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: How to Divide
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - How to Divide. You can either slice pieces off the edge of the plant or lift the whole clump and divide it (1). Some plants will just fall apart once they’re out of the ground, while for others you’ll need a sharp spade or soil knife (2) to create divisions. Just be sure that each piece has some roots and a few leaves.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Replanting Divisions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Replanting Divisions. Get the new divisions planted at the same depth they were growing in the ground or in a pot right away. You’ll want to keep them watered if it doesn’t rain so new roots get going and the foliage doesn’t get crispy. If your new division is in full sun, create some temporary shade so it doesn’t get cooked by the heat: Attach landscape fabric to a tomato cage and leave it in place for a week or so until the plant settles in.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Division Captions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Division captions. It was easy to pull apart the fibrous roots of this garden phlox with a garden fork (1). But in a couple of spots the roots were so thick that it took a knife (2) to get them apart. Give your new division a head start by placing it in the hole, then watering before filling the hole with soil and watering again.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Botanical Names for Division
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Botanical Names. Baptisia: Baptisia spp. and hybrids. Butterfly weed: Asclepias tuberosa. Daylily: Hemerocallis spp. and hybrids. Garden phlox: Phlox paniculata.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Dividing Garden Phlox
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Technique photos showing garden phlox division: lifting fibrous roots with a garden fork, cutting dense roots apart with a knife, and watering a newly placed division before backfilling.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Simple Layering
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Get More Shrubs with Simple Layering. Some shrubs will do this on their own if they have a low-growing branch touching the soil. This technique works for lots of woody plants, such as vines and shrubs. Look for flexible stems—roots form more easily on young growth.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: When to Layer
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - When to Layer. Any time of year will work, but fall or early spring is best because cooler temperatures and rain help them take off more quickly.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: How to Layer
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - How to Layer. You may be able to anchor a stem to the soil with a rock and the plant will root on its own. But to ensure growth, find a low-growing stem that’s 2 to 3 feet long. Dig a shallow 3- to 4-inch-deep hole just under the spot where you can bend it over to touch the ground. If there are leaves, strip them off of the portion that will be underground. Then cut a shallow 1-inch-long wound in that spot on the stem (1). Brush some rooting hormone on if you’d like and pin the stem in place (2).

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Staking a Layered Stem
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Staking a Layered Stem. Bend the tip upward and secure it to a stake to encourage upright growth (3). Refill the hole with soil and water thoroughly. Make sure the soil has settled in to cover the wound so it doesn’t dry out.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Give Them Time to Root
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Give Them Time to Root. It can take up to a year for roots to form, depending on the plant and the growing conditions. To check progress, carefully brush away the soil and pull up the landscape pin. Ideally, after a year of growing, there should be a nice cluster of roots and you can cut your new shrub away from the mother plant. But if you only see one or two roots, it’s a good idea to cover the stem and keep it attached for another season.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Whether you’re a propagation pro or new to the craft, give these easy techniques a try and you’ll be able to fill borders and containers without busting your budget. —Sherri Ribbey

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Sherri's Tip
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Sherri’s tip. Sherri likes to take advantage of the stems she accidentally breaks off when it’s time to plant her coleus and Swedish ivy. She pops them in some potting mix and has new plants in just a few weeks.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Shrubs to Layer
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants - Shrubs to Layer. Azalea: Rhododendron spp. and hybrids. Boxwood: Buxus spp. and hybrids. Clematis: Clematis spp. and hybrids. Climbing rose: Rosa spp. and hybrids. Common lilac: Syringa vulgaris. Forsythia: Forsythia x intermedia. Honeysuckle: Lonicera spp. and hybrids.

title: 3 Ways to Get Free Plants: Simple Layering
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Technique photos showing simple layering: cutting away the outer bark layer on a woody stem, pinning the wounded stem down before covering it with soil, and tying the stem tip to a stake for upright growth.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? We’ll help you grow just what you need! When I first started vegetable gardening, I would sow every single seed in the envelope and plant every seedling in the pack, take care of hundreds of my growing babies and struggle with letting any of them go. Oversowing and overplanting left me with more produce than I could handle and sometimes weird-looking, stunted crops that were growing too close together. There was no way everything that germinated would fit in my garden, but watching those little seeds sprout and turn into plants was a treat in itself.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Every year of experience with a vegetable garden helps you decide what to do the following year, but if you’re not sure if you’re planting enough or too much of a particular crop, start with the table on the right. It’ll help you decide whether to start with seeds or plants, how many to put in, and whether (and how much) to thin. If you’re getting started with vegetable gardening, this will help you mix and match your favorite crops into the space you have. These suggestions are based on fresh eating for a single person or a family of four, for four or five meals. You may decide you want to eat more than that, but it’s a starting point. If you’d like to freeze, can or pickle, decide how many meals you’d like to eat throughout the year and adjust accordingly.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Happy planting! —Marisa Reyes

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Marisa's Note
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Even though she knows better, Marisa still always goes overboard on tomatoes, but her family and friends never complain!

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Beans
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Beans: Plant 10 to 15 plants per 1 person or 40 to 45 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 2 to 3 in. Direct sow seeds. Comment: Plant successive crops every two weeks for a continuous harvest; great for canning and pickling.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Beets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Beets: Plant 10 to 12 plants per 1 person or 40 to 48 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 3 in. Direct sow seeds. Comment: Beets store well; plant in spring and fall for two harvests each year.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Broccoli
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Broccoli: Plant 1 to 2 plants per 1 person or 4 to 6 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 15 in. Transplant seedlings. Comment: Every time you cut a head, more smaller ones will form.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Cabbage
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Cabbage: Plant 2 to 3 plants per 1 person or 8 to 10 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 9 to 12 in. Direct sow seeds or transplant seedlings. Comment: Plant cabbage closer together for smaller heads.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Carrots
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Carrots: Plant 20 to 30 plants per 1 person or 80 to 90 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 1 to 2 in. Direct sow seeds. Comment: Long shelf life; plant in spring and fall for multiple harvests.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Celery
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Celery: Plant 1 to 2 plants per 1 person or 4 to 6 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 8 to 12 in. Transplant seedlings. Comment: Stronger taste than store bought; celery stalks will regrow after being cut.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Corn
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Corn: Plant 10 to 12 plants per 1 person or 40 to 48 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 12 in. Direct sow seeds. Comment: Plant in blocks for best pollination.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Cucumbers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Cucumbers: Plant 1 to 2 plants per 1 person or 3 to 4 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 12 to 24 in. Direct sow seeds or transplant seedlings. Comment: Plant 12 in. apart if using a trellis system and 24 in. apart if they’re rambling on the ground.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Lettuce
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Lettuce: Plant 4 to 6 plants per 1 person or 16 to 24 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 9 in. Direct sow seeds or transplant seedlings. Comment: Stagger sowing for one head per week per person.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Melons
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Melons: Plant 1 to 2 plants per 1 person or 2 to 4 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 24 in. Direct sow seeds. Comment: Plant two seeds per hole in mounds 24 inches apart.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Onions
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Onions: Plant 6 to 12 plants per 1 person or 24 to 48 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 4 to 6 in. Transplant seedlings. Comment: Buy sets (individual bulbs) or plants (in bundles) and plant two per person, per week.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Peas
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Peas: Plant 15 to 20 plants per 1 person or 60 to 80 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 2 in. Direct sow seeds or transplant seedlings. Comment: Grow peas on a trellis.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Peppers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Peppers: Plant 1 to 3 plants per 1 person or 1 to 12 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 12 to 24 in. Transplant seedlings. Comment: Most hot peppers are prolific: one plant is enough for one or four people; for larger peppers, grow two to three plants per person.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Potatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Potatoes: Plant 4 to 6 plants per 1 person or 12 to 24 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 12 in. Plant seed potatoes directly. Comment: Seed potatoes are tubers you plant in the ground; each plant will yield 1 lb. of potatoes.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Spinach
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Spinach: Plant 4 to 8 plants per 1 person or 16 to 32 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 3 to 6 in. Direct sow seeds or transplant seedlings. Comment: Plant in spring and fall for two harvests a year.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Squash
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Squash, summer + winter: Plant 1 to 2 plants per 1 person or 2 to 4 plants for 4 people. Thin seedlings to 18 to 36 in. Direct sow seeds or transplant seedlings. Comment: Plant summer squash 18 in. apart and larger plants of winter squash 36 in. apart.

title: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant?: Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: How Many Vegetables Should You Plant? Tomatoes: Plant 1 to 4 plants per 1 person or 1 to 16 plants for 4 people. Plant spacing is 12 to 24 in. Transplant seedlings. Comment: Cherries: Grow one per person; slicing: grow one to two per person; paste: grow three to four per person.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Opening garden photo for “Showstopping Curb Appeal,” showing a red brick home framed by mature trees, a front-yard island bed, spring tulips, daffodils, windflowers, shrubs, and a stone path.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Wide front-yard garden view with a red brick home, mature pin oaks, layered shrubs, spring bulbs, groundcovers, garden seating, and curving paths that create curb appeal.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: An Impressive Island Bed
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Learn the secrets to a front-yard garden with big impact! An Impressive Island Bed. Like many of us, Renee Minirth’s Memphis garden started with a few pass-along plants several years ago: Three English rose cuttings from her father-in-law. These few plants ignited Renee’s interest in gardening.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: An Impressive Island Bed
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - An Impressive Island Bed. Fast forward to 2015 when Renee’s family moved into their second house (and brought the roses), and her hobby blossomed. Renee decided to mostly start over on the front-yard landscaping because it appeared that drought and disease had taken their toll on the once-beautiful boxwoods and azaleas. She replanted the foundation plantings with new boxwoods and yews but every trip to the garden center revealed new plants that she wanted to try.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: An Impressive Island Bed
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - An Impressive Island Bed. And then the pandemic hit. Renee, a forensic psychiatrist, was working long, difficult hours and found herself spending the rest of her time at home. “I poured myself into the garden as a means of coping. Garden is my exercise, my mental relief and my art form,” she says.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Island Bed Design
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Island Bed Design. In spring 2021, Renee decided to expand the beds in the front yard. You can see the original pin oaks with small circles of ground cover and several lanky azaleas beneath them in the before photo at left. Renee played around with the idea of two islands but realized that this just wouldn’t be enough room for all of the plants that she had in mind. So in the end, she drew up a large kidney-shaped bed with a pathway through the middle that joined the two trees together.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Start with Structure
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Start with Structure. She cut back the old azaleas to rejuvenate them, then once another local gardener helped her identify them as ‘Girard’s Pleasant White,’ she added several more of that variety in a semicircle. Other shrubs snake through the bed in curving rows to give it background and structure. They include Sprinter® littleleaf boxwood, ‘Otto Luyken’ dwarf cherry laurel and Ivory Halo Tartarian dogwood. She bridged the gap between the tall pin oaks and lower-growing shrubs with ‘Appalachian Spring’ flowering dogwood, which was bred at the University of Tennessee and is well suited to the climate in this Memphis garden.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Botanical Names
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
