title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Planting Around Trees
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Planting Around Trees. If you’ve ever tried to plant a garden around an existing tree, you know that your first goal is to keep the established tree healthy. That’s why Renee was careful not to damage any large roots when she dug holes for the shrubs. Luckily, oak trees tend to have fewer surface roots than some, so it’s easier than it might have been under a different type of tree.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Add in Color
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Add in Color. Once Renee had the shape and structure of this front yard put together, she planted a combination of bulbs, annuals and perennials to keep a colorful show going from early spring through fall. It starts with the tulips in photo 1, and by summer, when the trees are all leafed out, she replaces them with shade-loving annuals, such as impatiens and coleus, and the colorful caladiums in photo 2. She’s able to dig up and save about a third of the caladiums from year to year, but others fade away and need to be replaced. The impact they make in this highly visible spot makes it worth the work.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Bulb Impact

content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Bulb Impact. As you can see, bulbs are a big part of what makes this garden so spectacular in spring.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Spring Bulb Favorites
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Spring Bulb Favorites. This garden has plenty to look at all year, but its spring show is especially impressive. Renee says that she planted 4,600 spring-blooming bulbs, including tulips and daffodils, a couple of years ago. You can see the results of that hard work on these pages. She doesn’t plant that many every year, as many return.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Planting Bulbs in Trenches
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Planting Bulbs in Trenches. If you’re planting in open bed space, the easiest way to plant large numbers of bulbs is to dig a trench in fall, drop in the bulbs and shovel soil over them. Put a mix of early, mid- and late-blooming varieties in the same trench and you’ll guarantee color for several weeks, or even months. Renee says that she gets the longest show out of early and midseason varieties because by the time the late tulips bloom, the weather is turning hot, which causes the flowers to fade faster. Trenching isn’t an option for every spot in this garden, so in the spaces between companion perennials, Renee digs bulbs in individually.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: A Few Favorites
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - A Few Favorites. Pink and blue are Renee’s favorite flower colors, so she starts with those two base colors, and usually adds accents of white and yellow. The pink tulips include early ‘Foxtrot’ and ‘Spring Green’ at left, midseason white-tinged-with-pink ‘Infinity’ and late-blooming ‘Sauternes.’ The cheerful Sunshine Boys™ daffodil blend at left is a terrific way to start the season, and fragrant white ‘Thalia’ daffodils are a favorite in midspring. Long-lasting blue, pink and white windflowers have multiplied beautifully along the borders. Finally, every year Renee likes to try some new surprises. This year she loved ‘Black Hero’ tulips, so they may make it into the regular rotation as well.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Returning Bulbs
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Returning Bulbs. Daffodils and windflowers return reliably and, in fact, multiply. While Renee doesn’t pull and replace the tulips, she also can’t count on them to return, so she adds more each fall to guarantee blooms, as they tend to fade out after a few years—and often get eaten by her nemesis, voles.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Tulips in Containers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Try Tulips in Containers. Tulips also make beautiful container plants. In photo 3, you can see how Renee keeps several simple pots tucked in an out-of-the-way spot all winter, and as each pot is about to burst into bloom, it’s ready to move to a spot on the patio or next to the front door. Another perfect use? Plant tulip bulbs in your vegetable beds and use them as cut flowers before you need the space for other plants later.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Container Caption
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Splash color around your garden. Containers are a great way to use up extra bulbs that you didn’t get into the ground in fall or show off those that you snag at end-of-season clearance sales.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Multiseason Appeal
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Multiseason Appeal. The mix of plants in this front yard ensures that there’s something beautiful to look at year-round. In spring it’s the bulbs and early emerging plants beneath still-leafless trees in photo 4. The structure of the repeated shrubs make a great backdrop, and by late spring, they have come into their own. Some favorite perennials in this shady front yard include coral bells, hostas, coneflowers and toad lilies, which bloom in late summer or fall. In photo 5 you can see that by summer, the panicle hydrangeas have reached their glory and make a big impact in that spot as well. What a welcome!

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Practical Matters
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Practical Matters. Gardening in Memphis definitely presents its challenges. There’s usually plenty of rainfall (although 2022 was an especially dry year), so Renee doesn’t irrigate very often, but lots of moisture paired with the characteristic Tennessee heat creates a different problem: fungal diseases. The few roses she grows in the backyard are especially susceptible to blackspot. But she doesn’t want to give up on them; they were her first plants, after all. So she starts spraying them with a copper fungicide in late winter, which helps, but by midsummer many have succumbed, so she leaves them alone and the following spring they re-emerge with fresh foliage.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Vole Control
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Vole Control. These little rodents eat bulbs, tunnel in the lawn and chew up perennial and shrub roots. However, Renee takes a big-picture approach: “I prefer to live with them and work with the natural order of things, so I encourage natural predators like owls and the two hawk families that live in the yard.” She refuses to use poison to kill the critters because she doesn’t want to hurt the birds. So she tries to live with the damage and protects the plants that they seem to hurt most: She often plants new hydrangeas in wire mesh baskets to protect the roots. But that isn’t a realistic solution for hundreds of bulbs. She’s discovered that a 12-inch-deep trench filled with sharp lava rock installed around bed edges seems to deter them, so she puts this in spots that are especially hard hit.

title: Showstopping Curb Appeal: Classic Hardscaping
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Classic Hardscaping. Plants aren’t the only thing that makes this garden so appealing. Brick walls, paths and pedestals add both repetition and punctuation to the design and create an alcove around the seating area in photos 6 and 7. Renee enjoys her morning coffee here, and it’s one of three benches tucked into different spots around the front yard, all offering unique views and a surprising amount of privacy. Renee calls the lamp next to this bench her “Narnia lamp.” It’s the perfect entrance to her garden escape. —Kristin Beane Sullivan

content: Showstopping Curb Appeal - Kristin’s note. Kristin agrees that gardening is good therapy, and finds digging into a big weeding or pruning project to be a great stress reliever. Is it the sun, the soil, the sense of accomplishment? Probably all of the above!

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Let our quiz help you find a fresh take on your garden style. Gardens don’t stay the same from year to year—we try new plants, tweak the layout, experiment with growing methods—that’s the fun of gardening. But every once in a while, we need some sparkling new ideas to motivate us. If you’re unsure about which is the next best step for your space, or if you simply want to be in tune with the gardening world’s most current obsessions, take the following quiz to determine your general gardening style. Then flip to your personalized inspiration page to uncover a tailored collection of trends that are sure to fit right in with your taste and preferences. Which new idea is waiting to hook you? —Chloe Deike

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Chloe's Note
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Chloe enjoys scoping out new, inspiring ideas while meandering through the gardens of friends, acquaintances and neighbors.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism. We’re all familiar with the term minimalism by now—the idea that less is more has been trendy for a while. But in the opposite way, a flowery maximalism garden style has a different goal: to fill every inch of available space with plants.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism. Take a stroll along the paths of this garden and run your hand through the blooming perennials. Notice vegetables ripening within the beds and borders while vining plants climb overhead. You might even be hit with some nostalgia as you spot a couple classic flowering shrubs, such as a common lilac or panicle hydrangea.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism. Though the overall look of the garden might lean a little bit wild, every plant is thoughtfully placed and boasts more than one beneficial quality, whether it produces a harvest, provides important nutrition for butterflies and bees or flowers prolifically.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism Care
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism care. A garden like this requires regular care from a knowledgeable gardener, but the maintenance tasks are simple and not very time consuming. Your main focus is building quality soil so that your plants grow strong, healthy and produce bountifully. If you don’t already compost, now is a good time to start.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism Trends
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism - The trends for you: Vegetables grown within ornamental borders; pollinator conscious and wildlife-friendly; nostalgic, timeless shrubs; bright and cheerful color scheme.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism Botanical Names
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism - Botanical Names. Common lilac: Syringa vulgaris. Common violet: Viola sororia. Panicle hydrangea: Hydrangea paniculata. White clover: Trifolium repens.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism Caption
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Flowery Maximalism caption. An abundant variety of plants makes a colorful and spirited scene with endless interest and numerous benefits — for yourself, your dinner table and for the wildlife.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Flowery Maximalism
author: Chloe Deike
content: Cottage-style flowery maximalism garden with dense layered plantings, blooming shrubs, a white fence, a birdhouse, and a narrow path through abundant perennials.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Bee Lawn
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Next Trend to Tackle: Bee Lawn. Replace your traditional turf lawn with a variety of low-growing perennials that pollinators love, such as white clover and common violet. This lawn swap will have more texture and color and literally buzz with life. Start the transition by tossing seed overtop of your existing lawn, preferably in fall, and the following season you’ll start to see an increase in your bee activity. Find seed and growing information online at Twin City Seed Co. (twincityseed.com).

title: Plant Profile: Lakota™ Fire Coneflower
author: Chloe Deike
content: Echinacea Lakota™ Fire. Here’s an example of a plant that does it all: continuous hot magenta-red summer blooms turn to bold, brown seedheads that birds love to feast on through winter. Lakota™ Fire grows 12 to 16 inches tall and 16 to 18 inches wide in full sun in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Plant Profile: 'Chicago Hardy' Fig
author: Chloe Deike
content: Ficus carica ‘Chicago Hardy’. Nothing seems as decadent and delectable as plucking a plump, ripe fig from the branch to bring inside for an appetizer. ‘Chicago Hardy’ is hardy in USDA zones 6 to 10, though it can be grown in zone 5 with protection. Its mature size is 10 to 15 feet tall and 9 to 12 feet wide.

title: Plant Profile: 'Sunset' Runner Bean
author: Chloe Deike
content: Phaseolus coccineus ‘Sunset’. The profuse, soft pink blooms of ‘Sunset’ are more subtle than the usual bright scarlet runner bean. Plant in full sun in spring when the soil is warmed. You’ll need a trellis or arbor to support the 6- to 7-foot-long vine. The beans can be prepared fresh or used dried.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Mindful Oasis
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Mindful Oasis. Nothing, not even the plants, are as important to this garden style as creating the right vibe. This type of garden is all about the experience, and its primary purpose is to provide a place of respite for all who visit. Step into this garden and you’ll feel like you’ve arrived at your own personal oasis.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Mindful Oasis Design
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Mindful Oasis design. The surest way to secure a comfortable, easy feeling in this garden is to design it so that maintenance needs are kept to a minimum. Hardscaping dominates the space and provides wide walkways and ample places to entertain or sit and relax. Plus it limits your growing space, forcing you to be particular about choosing a limited plant palette. Create plant groupings throughout the garden to create repetition.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Mindful Oasis Native Plants
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Mindful Oasis native plants. It’s easy to customize a garden like this to fit your region. Choose native plants whenever possible — they are well-adapted to your climate and weather, making them resilient and reliable without much fuss or extra care from you.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Mindful Oasis Trends
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Mindful Oasis - The trends you’ve aced: Outdoor living room; limited lawn space or lawn replacement; native plants; colorful foliage, minimal flowers.

author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Mindful Oasis - Botanical Names. Foxtail lily: Eremurus robustus. Japanese anemone: Anemone hupehensis. Red banana: Musa acuminata. Sago palm: Cycas revoluta.

author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Mindful Oasis caption. Plants are the accessories in this garden. Strong, straight lines and lots of stone and gravel make this scene easy to digest and immediately offer a sense of peace.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Plants That Move
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Next Trend to Tackle: Plants That Move. Set the tone of your garden with plants that add movement — ones that sway with a gentle wind, nod happily along or offer a soft rustling melody as they move. Any ornamental grass will do the trick, foxtail lily’s long tapering blooms tip back and forth, and Japanese anemone bob midborder. Tall plants are bound to catch a breeze, so choose one big-leafed tropical to pop in a planter, such as a Sago palm or red banana plant. Start with just a few plants with movement to create a subtle effect.

title: Plant Profile: 'Brilliance' Autumn Fern
author: Chloe Deike
content: Dryopteris erythrosora ‘Brilliance’. A native shade plant is sure to set your mind at ease as you relax outdoors. The new fronds emerge bright orange and fade throughout the summer. It grows 18 to 30 inches tall and wide in part to full shade in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Plant Profile: 'Emerald Mist' Brunnera
author: Chloe Deike
content: Brunnera macrophylla ‘Emerald Mist’. Silvery patterned leaves offer a nice cool tone to the garden, and bright blue clusters of tiny flowers in spring cheerfully dance above. You can grow this in part to full shade in USDA zones 3 to 8. Expect it to get 12 to 15 inches tall and wide.

title: Plant Profile: Prairie Dropseed
author: Chloe Deike
content: Sporobolus heterolepis. Fine leaves of this native perennial grass cascade like silk toward the ground. In late summer, flowers shoot above the droopy foliage, and their feathery purple-tinted blooms wave along with the late-season breeze. It grows in full sun in USDA zones 3 to 8 and will reach 2 to 3 feet tall and wide.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Elegant Drama
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Elegant Drama. Unashamed of its lines of trees, expansive lawn and winding hedges, this garden is one of grand distinction. It can tend toward a historic and formal look with tidy hedges. Beds are well-defined, everything is kept trim and neat, and plants are chosen for their ability to generate contrast and drama, such as using dark foliage and bright white blooms. Plus, this garden style is ripe with historic design concepts that certainly give your garden a sense of importance.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Elegant Drama
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Elegant Drama. Modern versions of this garden meld together several popular garden trends of the past and don’t stick to just one time period. Contained within sharp-edged borders and tucked among the hedges, you’ll discover little collections of colorful plants. Take an up-close peek and you’ll notice patterned foliage and spotted, dotted or striped flowers beloved in Victorian times.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Elegant Drama Care
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Elegant Drama care. You probably prefer a stable, consistent look so you’ll need to be willing to put in the regular effort to maintain a tidy garden (or hire somebody who can).

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Elegant Drama Trends
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Elegant Drama - The trends for you: Plants with dark foliage and light blooms; variegated foliage and patterned flowers; neatly trimmed evergreen shrubs and trees.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Elegant Drama Caption
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Elegant Drama caption. A booming return of historic garden practices reflects a growing desire to use our gardens to create impressive artistic expressions.

title: Which Garden Trends Suit You?: Add Some Topiary
author: Chloe Deike
content: Which Garden Trends Suit You? Next Trend to Tackle: Add Some Topiary. Don’t be intimidated to try your hand at this timeless garden art form. You’ll need an evergreen shrub or small tree and some pruners. Choose from a spiral or spherical shape to begin, and grow it in a container so that you can rotate the best side forward in case you make some small mistakes. As you hone your craft, you can branch out into more complex shapes. Maybe someday you’ll be growing an evergreen replica of your favorite pet!

title: Plant Profile: 'Black Negligee' Bugbane
author: Chloe Deike
content: Actaea simplex ‘Black Negligee’. Deep purple-black foliage anchors this perennial to the landscape. Long, soft white flowers up to 5 feet tall wave in the breeze for an elegant touch. They bloom in fall in USDA zones 4 to 8 and grow 4 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide in part shade.

title: Plant Profile: Nitty Gritty™ White Rose
author: Chloe Deike
content: Rosa Nitty Gritty™ White. Bright white, frilly blooms add a touch of romance. Let them scramble in front of a tall hedge. They’ll rebloom from spring to fall in USDA zones 4 to 9 and grow 3 to 4 feet tall and wide in full sun.

title: Plant Profile: 'Silver Edge' Siberian Iris
author: Chloe Deike
content: Iris sibirica ‘Silver Edge’. This soft blue beauty with a white picotee edge is reminiscent of Victorian times. Leave the seedheads after it blooms in late spring for interest later in the season. It grows 2 to 3 feet tall and wide in full sun to part shade in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: From the Test Garden: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots. To start seeds and get young plants growing, I’ve always defaulted to the traditional plastic pot. But I’ve gotten tired of cleaning and storing an ever-growing pile of nonrecycleable pots. So in the interest of using less plastic, I searched out biodegradable pot options. I wanted to know how they compare: Were they easy to use? Did they inhibit root growth? Did they break down in one growing season?

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: The Test
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - The Test. For this admittedly unscientific, anecdotal experiment, I planted Xochi Orange marigolds (Tagetes hybrid) in eight different kinds of biodegradable pots. I started them indoors in the same potting mix under the same lights, and watered and fertilized them at the same time and grew them there for almost 10 weeks — longer than I planned to, but the weather wasn’t cooperating for transplanting. I was surprised to note that my seedlings all grew quite differently indoors, as you can see in the photo at right. But once planted outdoors (pot and all) in a raised bed, the marigolds all evened out within a couple of weeks and I couldn’t tell the difference between them.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: End-of-Season Results
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - End-of-Season Results. At the end of the season after a frost, I dug up the plants. Some roots appeared slightly obstructed by the container materials, growing over the top or through the bottom drainage holes, but all of the plants had grown and thrived. And though in varying states of decomposition, I could still identify each pot by its remains. Most were easily crumbled apart and scattered into the garden, while others will need to spend a season in my compost pile to break down further. Either way, I don’t have to store pots! Check out my findings here. —Jennifer Howell

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Material Types
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - Biodegradable Material. A: Peat or fiber pots, square packs: molded multi-packs made of peat or wood fiber. B: Peat or coir expandable pellets: compressed peat or coir shaped by mesh covering, expands when wet. C: Toilet paper roll: cardboard tube from inside of toilet paper or paper towel roll. D: Peat pot: molded round pots made of peat. E: DIY paper pot: rolled strips of newspaper or paper grocery bag with crimped bottom. F: Fabric pot: nonwoven biodegradable fabric pouch. G: Recycled paper box: paperboard box with matching tray to hold multiple boxes. H: Honeycomb paper flat: lightweight paper planting cells glued together and folded accordion-style pull apart into a full flat-sized grid.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Peat and Fiber Pots
author: Jennifer Howell

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Peat or Fiber Pots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - A, peat or fiber pots, square packs. Getting started: Easy to fill and plant; pots fit in any standard-sized flat or a variety of trays. Growing and transplanting: Pot got wet and soft but held its shape; easy to separate cells; planted so entire pot was underground so it didn’t wick moisture from root ball. What remained: Mostly intact but decayed. Pros and cons: Easy to find and inexpensive; many sizes available; peat pots broke down faster than fiber.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Peat or Coir Expandable Pellets
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - B, peat or coir expandable pellets. Getting started: Easy to soak discs in accompanying leak-proof tray; mesh obstructed seed planting; no extra mix to cover seed. Growing and transplanting: Roots grew through the mesh and out the bottom where they tangled together, but teased apart easily to plant. What remained: Mesh still intact around coir or peat core. Pros and cons: Can’t choose your potting mix; leak-proof tray has no drainage and is easy to overwater.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Toilet Paper Roll
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - C, toilet paper roll. Getting started: Cut and folded bottom to create pot; pots didn’t always sit level; was easy to scoop and fill. Growing and transplanting: Dried out quickly but also prone to getting moldy if watered too much; harder for roots to penetrate than other materials. What remained: Still intact but tore apart easily when damp. Pros and cons: Virtually free; took time to make; cardboard tube would sometimes unwrap at the top.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Peat Pot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - D, peat pot. Getting started: Easy to scoop and fill with potting mix and plant; pots fit in variety of flats or trays. Growing and transplanting: Moist peat softened so roots grew through, but if dry, it hardened and could inhibit roots; if the top of the pot wasn’t buried, moisture could wick out. What remained: Peat still visible but deteriorated. Pros and cons: Inexpensive and available in lots of sizes; crumbled easily to work into soil as organic matter.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: DIY Paper Pot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - E, DIY paper pot. Getting started: Easy to make but slow; had to pour potting mix into the pot — can’t scoop to fill because paper is crushable. Growing and transplanting: Dried out quickly; when wet, paper was mushy and harder to handle. What remained: Crumbled bits barely there. Pros and cons: Nice way to recycle paper; can form pots on a drinking glass or buy a tool at gardeners.com.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Fabric Pot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - F, fabric pot. Getting started: Hard to fill because bag was flimsy and wouldn’t stand open when empty; tipped over easily. Growing and transplanting: Roots grew through the bag very easily, which made it hard to remove the bag to plant if you wanted to. What remained: Totally intact after one season. Pros and cons: Very inexpensive; ships flat; can write on bag; needs light to break down or it will take several seasons.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Recycled Paper Box
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - G, recycled paper box. Getting started: Folded boxes pop open with little effort; durable enough to scoop soil; easy to drop in seed and cover. Growing and transplanting: Boxes got soft but handled and transplanted with no trouble; roots struggle to grow through the cardboard, but perforated bottoms tear off easily to allow growth. What remained: Intact but cardboard was crumbling. Pros and cons: Ships folded flat with minimal packaging waste; can write on the box to label plants.

title: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots: Honeycomb Paper Flat
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Breakdown on Biodegradable Pots - H, honeycomb paper flat. Getting started: Required a special-sized perforated flat and tool to hold the accordion paper in place until filled with potting mix; was easy to plant. Growing and transplanting: Easy to move as a unit in the heavy-duty flat, but not as individual cells; paper got damp and tore off easily when transplanting; roots grew out the bottomless cells and tangled. What remained: Partially intact, but deteriorated. Pros and cons: Initial investment of special flat and separating tool is pricey but accordion refills inexpensive and ship flat; hard to plant a partial flat.

title: Q&A: Removing Perennial Sweet Pea Vines
author: Thelma Homer, NV
content: Q&A - Removing perennial sweet pea vines. Q: Help! How do I get rid of perennial sweet pea vines? They’re invasive! —Thelma Homer, NV. A: Perennial, or everlasting, sweet pea (Lathyrus latifolius) spreads by seeds and rhizomes. And it also has a tough taproot. This will be an ongoing challenge to remove and could take several years. First, prevent it from setting seeds, which are poisonous. When the seeds are ripe, the pod ejects them up to 30 feet! And the seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to five years. Keep mowing or cutting sprouts as you see them. Unfortunately, because the plant spreads by both rhizomes and a taproot, you can’t just pull it; you’ll have to dig. Covering the area with plastic and mulch will also help reduce sprouts. But they still may creep out at the edges. Finally, broadleaf and nonselective herbicides are an option. But be vigilant and spray young sprouts as soon as you see them.

title: Garden Jargon: Etiolated
content: Garden Jargon - Etiolated. As you uncover the garden in spring, you might find spindly yellow or white foliage like the sedum in the photo below. It is etiolated because it’s been deprived of light. Once exposed to the sun, chlorophyll changes it to green.

title: Q&A: Rotting a Tree Stump
author: Al Sabers, TN
content: Q&A - Rotting a tree stump. Q: I have a tree stump in a hard-to-reach spot. How can I get it to rot quickly without grinding? —Al Sabers, TN. A: Pack a stump-rotting product into the wood to help it decompose faster. You have a few options: You can buy a product specifically for this purpose, which usually contains potassium nitrate, at the garden center. Or you can use any high-nitrogen fertilizer. Finally, if pets seem to be attracted to the stump, yeast nutrient used in wine making is a safe alternative. Cut the stump off as close to soil level as possible. If it’s damp, let it dry. Next, drill several holes at least 1/2 inch in diameter and several inches deep. Pack the holes full of rotting product, then soak the ground around the stump and sprinkle the surface to moisten the material in the holes. Next lay a sheet of plastic over the area and weigh down the corners. Finally, spread a layer of organic mulch to shade it and help keep it moist under the plastic. Check the stump occasionally and moisten it if it’s dry to encourage decomposition. In a couple of months, the stump should soften to the point that it’ll crumble into chunks you can easily remove.

title: Q&A: Alternate-Blooming Flowering Crabapple
author: Margaret Kent, OH
content: Q&A - Alternate-blooming flowering crabapple. Q: Some years my ‘David’ flowering crabapple blooms better than others. Is there anything I can do to help it bloom better every year? —Margaret Kent, OH. A: Nope, it’s genetic. Several flowering crabapple (Malus hybrids) cultivars, including ‘David,’ ‘Dolgo,’ ‘Eleyi,’ ‘Katherine,’ ‘Van Eseltine’ and sargent flowering crabapples (M. sargentii) are alternate bloomers. You’ll see a lush flower show and lots of fruit one year, but the following year it will have a much lighter bloom.

title: Q&A: Spring Cleanup and Beneficial Insects
author: Carlie White, NJ
content: Q&A - Spring cleanup and beneficial insects. Q: I’ve heard that spring garden cleanup can disturb overwintering beneficial insects. When can I safely start? —Carlie White, NJ. A: Dead plants provide winter hiding places for lady beetles, fireflies, ground beetles and other helpful insects. Hollow stems shelter many native bees, and hungry birds peck through the tangle for a meal. To help all of these creatures, it’s best to wait until nighttime temps regularly stay in the 50s, about the time you mow your lawn the first time in spring or when fruit trees bloom in your area. If you start earlier and want to protect the insects, loosely pile the debris in an out-of-the-way spot, and they’ll still be able to emerge. One exception: If your garden had foliage disease or harmful insects, send that debris away in the trash in the fall to minimize the damage in following years.

title: Weed Watch: Nimblewill
content: Weed Watch - Nimblewill, Muhlenbergia schreberi. What it looks like: This fine-textured native perennial grass can grow up to 24 inches tall, but in turf areas the wiry stems are kept shorter because of mowing. However, you might not notice it in your lawn until cold weather arrives. Then the sprawling, densely branched mats of warm-season grass turn brown faster than most turfgrasses, as you can see above, and it remains brown until spring. From midsummer into fall, narrow heads, or panicles, rise just above the leaves loaded with tiny flowers that form lots of seeds. Even if the plant is mowed, it will continue to produce seeds.

title: Weed Watch: Nimblewill Habitat and Control
content: Weed Watch - Nimblewill, Muhlenbergia schreberi. Where to find it: Nimblewill hides best in lawns, but seeds also sprout in beds, borders and vegetable gardens. Tolerant of shade to full sun, moist to dry conditions, it’s happy almost anywhere. How to get rid of it: You can easily pull or hoe it from beds and borders. In a lawn, rake over a cluster to gather stems before pulling or digging. Be sure you get all of the pieces or it will quickly regrow. Nonselective herbicides will kill it, but they also kill plants it has sprawled into. Selective herbicides, such as mesotrione, are effective in cool-season turfgrasses. Apply it in summer when the weed is actively growing. However, it’s best to contact a lawn professional to be sure it’s safe to use on your turf.

title: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Editor’s Choice - Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade. With so many azaleas on the market it can be hard to choose, but you can’t go wrong with tried-and-true ‘Hino-Crimson.’ This award-winning variety packs a punch when it explodes with trusses of scarlet red blooms that completely cover the shrub in early spring. The small glossy-green leaves develop a bronze cast in winter and plants hold onto them until new growth begins again in spring.

title: Plant Profile: 'Hino-Crimson' Azalea
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Rhododendron hybrid. Shrub. Blooms: Clusters of single, crimson-red flowers in early to midspring. Light: Part to full shade. Soil: Moist, well-drained. Pests: Occasional rust or powdery mildew. Size: 2 to 4 ft. tall, 3 to 4 ft. wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 5 to 8. Source: Local garden centers.

title: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade: Root Matters
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade - Root Matters. Grow this azalea in dappled light with protection from the afternoon sun so the foliage won’t burn. Azaleas have shallow roots so when you plant, set the crown at the same depth it was growing in the pot to avoid smothering the roots or causing the plant to rot. A 1- to 2-inch layer of mulch helps retain moisture and keep soil temperatures even. As with many spring-blooming shrubs, a cold snap can jeopardize the blooms, so if you’re expecting temps below 25 degrees F and your ‘Hino-Crimson’ has fat buds or is blooming, toss a sheet or landscape fabric over it to save the flowers.

title: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade: Pruning Tips
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade - Pruning Tips. ‘Hino-Crimson’ doesn’t need much pruning. Remove any dead branches in spring but wait until after it flowers to shape the shrub so you don’t risk cutting off next year’s buds. If powdery mildew or rust have been a problem in the past, remove a few stems from the center to thin the growth and encourage better air circulation. Deadheading isn’t strictly necessary but can help tidy this shrub up after flowers fade. Just pinch spent blooms off with your fingertips.

title: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade: Plant Partners
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade - Plant Partners. The vibrant blooms of ‘Hino-Crimson’ are real attention getters. It’s a no-brainer as a specimen but fits in well with other border companions too. Check out “Burst of Spring Color” below if you want to start your growing season off with a bang. —Marisa Reyes

title: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade: Burst of Spring Color
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bring Dramatic Spring Color to Shade - Burst of Spring Color. Early spring brings loads of blooms from ‘Hino-Crimson’ azalea and the dainty white flowers of summer snowflake scattered below. A little later, the tight fiddleheads of interrupted fern push through the soil. As temperatures keep rising and summer arrives, spring flowers are replaced by astilbe’s tall violet-red plumes. Even after the color has faded, the blooms provide interest and structure until frost.

title: Plant Profile: Interrupted Fern

content: Osmunda claytoniana. Perennial with lush green divided fronds. Light: Full to part shade. Size: 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Woodland Sanctuary
content: Wouldn’t you love to wander down the path of this woodland getaway next spring? Lean down and marvel at the unique shape of the shooting star and fernleaf bleeding heart flowers. Breathe in the sweet scent of the woodland phlox (and watch spring butterflies like swallowtails enjoy them, as well!). Look for fuzzy new leaves emerging from the hydrangea stems. Listen for bird calls and look for nests of fledglings that may enjoy the berries of the European cranberrybush and downy serviceberry come summer.

title: Woodland Sanctuary: Design and Care
content: Woodland Sanctuary. Because this natural-looking design doesn’t require much fussing, you’ll be able to take time to enjoy the details instead of attending to them. These plants will do best in part shade. If your yard backs up to a wooded area, this would be perfect at its edge. Or if you are lucky enough to have tall trees with a high canopy, it’ll look right at home, and the plants should thrive. Install a curving mulched path and a few stones here and there to accent the garden. Let clumps of perennials grow together and weave around each other. As the seasons come and go, plants (and winged visitors) will too.

title: Woodland Sanctuary: Meet the Plants
content: Woodland Sanctuary - Meet the Plants. This mix of plants will feed birds and butterflies from spring through fall. And the casual arrangement of plants requires only a few cleanup tasks throughout the year. Start by cutting back and raking up perennial stems and fallen leaves in early spring. Be sure to get this out of the way before early-to-emerge brunnera flowers start. Later, you may decide to cut back the woodland phlox stems as they fade (a string trimmer may be the easiest way to do this as the clump grows) and the brunnera blooms to allow the foliage to take center stage. As summer turns to fall, cut back the hosta bloom stalks for a tidier look. Only prune the shrubs if there’s a broken or dead branch—no need to prune for shape or size.

title: A Garden for Every Season
content: No matter when you look out your window, this garden will have something to catch your eye. In winter, it’ll be the interesting branch structure of the Japanese maple, the evergreen foliage of the Hicks yew and even the flowers of the common snowdrops. Spring will bring azalea and hellebore blooms along with emerging hosta and sedge foliage. Summer offers up dramatic foliage contrasts and flowers of panicle hydrangeas, hostas and tuberous begonias. As the garden season winds down in autumn, this bed’s Japanese maple, hosta and sedge will light it up in shades of orange-red and yellow. Even gardens in part shade can have plenty of color, no matter what the season! Hardscaping elements like crisp edging, gently curving paths and welcoming arbors help, too.

title: A Garden for Every Season: Snowdrop Callout
content: A Garden for Every Season - Snowdrop callout. Plant handfuls of common snowdrop bulbs in spots that may be bare by late winter. Over time, they’ll spread into beautiful sweeps.

title: A Garden for Every Season: Yew and Hydrangea Callouts
content: A Garden for Every Season - Yew and hydrangea callouts. Hicks yew has a naturally upright habit. But if you need to prune it to maintain a smaller size or shape, prune in late winter or early spring. Panicle hydrangea blooms start white in summer and turn dusty pink by fall.

title: A Garden for Every Season: Planting Plan
author: Carlie Hamilton
content: Planting-plan diagram for A Garden for Every Season, with lettered plant groups around a path, arbors, and containers, plus callouts for Hicks yew and panicle hydrangea.

title: A Garden for Every Season: Meet the Plants
content: A Garden for Every Season - Meet the Plants. Not only does this garden look great in every season, but the plants don’t need much help from you to perform their best. Spend an afternoon in early spring pruning off dead hosta, fern, sedge and hellebore foliage, cutting back any winter-damaged hydrangea stems and raking up fallen leaves to tidy the garden. When the weather’s reliably above 50 degrees F, bring out your pots of tuberous begonias.

title: A Garden for Every Season: Watering
content: A Garden for Every Season - Watering. Especially in the first year or two, be sure the bed has an inch of water or so each week to help plants get established. After that, water only when they begin to suffer—sedge leaves may begin to turn brown or hellebore foliage may flop. Don’t rely on the hydrangea to tell you when the garden needs water. Its leaves may droop in the heat even with plenty of soil moisture.

title: A Garden for Every Season: Deer Protection
content: A Garden for Every Season - Deer protection. If deer are a problem in your garden, you may need to spray the yew, hydrangea, azalea and hosta with a repellent, as deer seem to find these plants especially attractive. As you can see, it’s not much work for a year’s worth of enjoyment!

title: from the editor
content: Sometimes when people show me or tell me about their gardens, they’re apologetic, as if they think I might judge its appearance. Believe me... I won’t. I definitely have no room to judge anyone else’s garden.

title: from the editor
content: For starters, my astilbes have looked rough for years. I’ve always known that they weren’t getting enough moisture. Our story on page 40 has inspired me to move these perennials to a spot where they can reach their full potential. And it also has me thinking that I may need a few more of these long-blooming beauties. I want a gorgeous sweep of them like Nima Marsh’s above!

title: from the editor
content: And sometimes the containers that I picture as I’m wandering the aisle of the garden center just don’t meet expectations later on. That’s why I love all of the ideas that our readers shared in the 2023 Container Challenge on page 54. So many terrific color and texture combos and care tips... and we know they work!

title: from the editor
content: This year, when someone walks by and complements the garden, I’ll just try to say “thank you” instead of immediately noticing, and maybe even pointing out, the burnt-up astilbes that I should have moved years ago, the mulch that the chickens kicked onto the sidewalk or the witchhazel that’s dying branch by branch. If I happen to visit your garden (and I hope I will!), know that I’m definitely not looking at all the little things that drive you crazy. I’m appreciating your beautiful entry containers, your impressive crop of jalapeños and the color on your Japanese maple leaves. I hope you are too.

title: A fishy solution
author: Jim Fameree, WI
content: To prevent birds from making nests in unsafe or inconvenient spots, Jim found that he could use two unexpected items: an old tuna can and a golf ball. In some spots, such as the one where a gutter or light attaches to siding, he just balances a can where the birds will knock it off if they try to land. It makes a clanging noise that scares them away. If they’re trying to build nests on the flat tops of his lights, he secures the can to the top. Then he places a golf ball inside. The ball rolls around when birds try to land and nest, startling them and sending them off to a different location.

title: Planter swapping system
author: Richard Sunberg, OH
content: It’s more economical to change your containers from season to season when you are growing some of the plants from seed. Richard has a simple rotating system in place to keep his front yard container display stunning: At the same time he plants up the spring containers in the front yard, he plants seeds and seedlings in a few pots in the backyard too. By the time the containers out front are fading, the seed-grown plants in the back have come into their own. Richard swaps the faded planters for fresh ones that keep his front entrance looking its best. Then in the backyard he refreshes the faded pots, pulling out some spent plants, replenishing potting mix and reseeding the empty spaces with cool-season plants that will be ready to show off by the time fall comes and he’s ready to swap the containers again.

title: Slug and snail deterrent
author: Constance Larson, ID
content: Constance has a problem with slugs and snails eating her hostas, so she applies ground eggshells to the areas around her hostas to deter the pests. To make the process easier, she realized she could reuse a grated parmesan cheese shaker — the durable plastic kind that dispenses from holes in the lid. Just wash the container out and let it fully dry before filling with clean, dry, ground eggshells.

title: A neighborly growing space
author: Kent Young, IA
content: If you are lacking space for a vegetable garden, you might want to team up. Kent and his neighbor both wanted a vegetable garden and decided that the flattest and sunniest location was where their side yards met. Together they built the raised bed in three stair-stepping sections to follow the slope of the yard, each with their own trellises. Then they each chose one section to plant and tend themselves, leaving the middle section for shared crops. Pole beans and cucumbers grow on the trellises that also help support tomatoes and peppers. Plus there’s always room to tuck in a few flowers. This has worked so well that they often have a big harvest they can share with friends and family.

title: Box tree moth
content: Another boxwood (Buxus spp. and hybrids) pest has entered the United States. It’s been spotted in New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan, Ohio and South Carolina. The adults have a 1 1/2-inch wingspan and the larvae hide in silky webs between boxwood leaves, euonymus or holly. They eat the leaves and can girdle and kill the shrub. If you suspect a box tree moth in your garden, try to catch one and keep it in a plastic bag, then call your local extension office. You can hand pick caterpillars and dispose of them in soapy water, or spray the plants with insecticidal soap, Bt, Spinosad or, with caution, broad spectrum caterpillar pesticides.

title: Rusty fire pit planter
author: Anna Ellenberger, PA
content: Instead of tossing out your old metal fire pit, line it with landscape fabric or coir lining and plant it up! Anna’s old fire pit had a few holes caused by rust that could provide drainage. But if yours doesn’t, just carefully drill a few new ones. If the exterior is looking a little rusty, a couple layers of spray paint can give it a fresh new look.

title: Spring into Summer with Easy-Care Combos

title: Spring into Summer with Easy-Care Combos
author: Jennifer Howell
content: There’s a time between the cool-season spring bulbs and heat-loving summer annuals when many perennials explode into bloom. It’s a joy to be in the garden: the temperature is warm but not hot, there’s been enough rain but it’s not muddy, and you’re still ahead of the weeds. The three plantings here hit their peak at that sweet spot between spring and summer.

title: Spring into Summer with Easy-Care Combos
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Want to keep these beauties looking great through the summer? Spread a 2- to 3-inch layer of mulch, such as shredded bark, wood chips, straw or even compost, around the plants before they get too big. This will help them stay hydrated and smother weed seedlings that would become competition in the garden. You’ll thank yourself later when you have fewer weeds to deal with and you won’t have to water as much. And don’t forget to deadhead to keep the plants looking tidy, extend their flowering time and encourage another flush of blooms.

title: Calming Pastel Palette
content: Groupings of low, mounded foliage topped by petite pastel flowers give this border a calming flow. Even without a glamorous, attention-getting plant as a focal point, your eye is drawn to the restful scene. And each of these perennials is a dependable, easy-care bloomer. Give them full sun and regular watering and they won’t let you down.

title: Calming Pastel Palette
content: Though this combo peaks in late spring to early summer, don’t think its show is one and done. Deadheading is the key to keeping it fresh and colorful. Cut lady’s mantle flower stems off at the base once they begin to turn brown to keep it tidy. Use scissors or a cordless hand-held hedge trimmer to shear spent blooms from catmint and dianthus after the first flush fades to coax a second, lighter bloom. Snip faded salvia spikes off just above a set of leaves to encourage secondary blooms to take off. Then, in midsummer if the plant is flopping or looking leggy, cut spent stems back to a few inches from the ground, where a mound of new growth will fill in and rebloom in late summer to fall alongside the pollinator-friendly seven-son flower.

title: Calming Pastel Palette: Seven-son flower
content: Seven-son flower, Heptacodium miconioides Temple of Bloom Tree, has white midsummer flowers with bracts that age to red in fall after petals drop. It grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 6 to 10 feet tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Calming Pastel Palette: Salvia
content: Salvia ‘Back to the Fuchsia’ is a perennial with pink flower spikes that rise up from mounded foliage from late spring to early fall. It grows 22 to 24 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Calming Pastel Palette: Catmint
content: Catmint, Nepeta ‘Cat’s Pajamas’, is a perennial with mounded gray-green foliage and lavender-blue flowers from late spring to early summer. It grows in full sun, reaches 12 to 14 inches tall and 18 to 20 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Calming Pastel Palette: Lady’s mantle
content: Lady’s mantle, Alchemilla mollis, is a perennial with chartreuse green mounded foliage and foamy yellow flowers in late spring to early summer. It grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 10 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 30 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Calming Pastel Palette: Dianthus
content: Dianthus ‘Red Rouge’ is a perennial with compact mounds of foliage topped by fragrant wine-red blooms edged and flecked with pink in early summer and early fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 6 to 8 inches tall and 14 to 20 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Spring into Summer with Easy-Care Combos
content: Narrow continuation crop of the spring-to-summer border photo shown beside the Calming Pastel Palette plant list.

title: An Easy Trade-Off
content: The vivid contrast of violet-purple giant allium blooms against burgundy barberry foliage is simple, but eye-catching. As giant allium flowers fade, foliage begins to yellow and go dormant. Just tuck it under the plume poppy’s coarse-textured leaves to hide it. Deer and rabbits leave this planting alone, and it requires almost no maintenance. Deadhead spent plume poppy blooms if you don’t want it to reseed. Prune barberry occasionally in early spring just to maintain its size or shape.

title: Gold Medal Worthy
content: Towering over all the rest of the plants in this border, Olympic mullein makes a bold statement with statuesque candelabras of yellow flowers in early summer over clumps of massive leaves. Cut back spent blooms, but leave a few to set seed. This short-lived perennial can take up to three years to bloom, then dies back, so letting it reseed ensures you’ll have more of these outstanding flowers year after year. Plant Zahara XL Yellow zinnia nearby to repeat the cheery color of the mullein. These workhorses supply nonstop flowers all summer until frost with just a bit of deadheading to keep them going strong. Complement them with cool blue-lavender Beth’s Blue laurentia for a winning color combination.

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
author: Tera Boeuf
content: If you’ve always dreamed of a beautiful hayrack planter dripping with flowers under your window but weren’t sure how to execute it, Tera Boeuf of Tera’s Gardens in Colorado can help. She has the secrets to planting and maintaining hayracks and is willing to share them with us!

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Large hayrack planter photo showing a dense, color-saturated windowbox display.

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Like siding, it’s a good idea to mount a hayrack with spacers to prevent moisture from building up between the planter and the siding. A 1 1/2-inch spacer block at the top and bottom of the hayrack should be enough to allow air to circulate and prevent rot.

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
author: Tera Boeuf
content: You can find hayracks in many sizes, but as with any container, the bigger it is, the heavier it is. Add soil and plants and it’ll be much tougher to mount. So it’s best to mount the empty hayrack and plant it up right where it hangs.

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Sometimes it’s hard to get watering just right. Tera tells people that if leaves look dull, they may need water, but if they’re yellowing, they’re probably getting too much water. This is more common than you might expect. Pick up a moisture meter from your garden center to help gauge your watering habits.

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Well-fed flowers bloom better. Whether you fertilize seems to be more important than what you use, so whatever you choose, just follow the package instructions for amount and frequency. Getting a great start is the key to Tera’s stunning hayrack creations.

title: The Secrets to Stunning Hayrack Planters
content: Second hayrack planter photo showing the same planting from another angle with pink and purple trailing flowers.

title: 3 Steps to Perfect Hayracks
author: Tera Boeuf
content: The biggest secret to Tera’s hayrack planter success is in the planting method. If you’ve ever wondered how to keep the soil in or how to get plants to trail the way you want them to, here are Tera’s steps for planting the perfect hayrack. Line the planter with a coco liner or sphagnum moss and bird netting, then fill it with potting mix and let it settle. Leave some room at the top of the planter before you start adding plants.

title: 3 Steps to Perfect Hayracks
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Diagram and supporting images showing the coco liner, sphagnum liner and planting-pocket setup for hayracks.

title: 3 Steps to Perfect Hayracks: Prepare the front
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Prepare the front of the hayrack with planting pockets so the planter itself nearly disappears. If you’re using a coco liner, use kitchen shears to cut a slit one shear length long at the top of every gap in the hayrack. Then toward the bottom of that cut, make another shorter angled cut to create a notch for each plant’s stem. In sphagnum, snip a hole in the bird netting and spread a space in the sphagnum to insert the plant’s rootball. Good plants for this front-row treatment include trailing petunias, ivy geraniums, impatiens, tuberous begonias and vining foliage plants such as vinca and creeping Jenny.

title: 3 Steps to Perfect Hayracks: Rinse & plant
author: Tera Boeuf
content: Tera likes to wash the potting mix from the roots of plants she tucks into the front of the hayrack. This makes it easier to fit the plants into the small slits or holes and lets her pack more of them into a small space. If you’re using 4-inch pots, slip in one plant per slit or hole; if you’re using multipacks, you can squeeze a couple of plants into each hole. Once the front has been planted, add plants to the middle and back, fill in around them with potting mix and water thoroughly to settle the mix around the roots.

title: Reasons to Get the Blues
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Blue is such a versatile garden color: dark blues tend to recede into the background, adding the illusion of space in a small garden. Its serene, calming vibe is perfect for a garden where you want to relax. Or plant blue flowers with complementary colors like orange or yellow to create energy and excitement. Pair blue and white for sharp, cool contrast. And you can add blue flowers to pastel plantings so they become more vibrant.

title: Reasons to Get the Blues
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In addition to all the visual reasons to use blue in your garden, one of the best perks is that pollinators love them. Bees are especially attracted to blue, and many butterflies and hummingbirds like blue blossoms almost as much as their traditional red favorites. And fortunately, there’s a blue flower for every season, from early spring to late fall, so you can draw these vital pollinating visitors to your garden for months. In this collection of beautiful blue flowers, there’s sure to be a few that will make you happy to get the blues.

title: ‘Nikko Blue’ bigleaf hydrangea
content: Hydrangea macrophylla ‘Nikko Blue’ produces some of the most intense blue blooms of all bigleaf hydrangeas, but soil type is critical. Bigleaf hydrangeas can be pink in color if the soil is alkaline, but will be blue in response to aluminum in acid soil. Do a soil test to determine your soil’s pH, and if it is higher than 5.5, add 1 Tbsp. aluminum sulfate to a gallon of water and water the hydrangea once a month starting in early spring to promote blue blooms.

title: ‘Nikko Blue’ bigleaf hydrangea
content: This hydrangea rarely needs pruning: just cut out dead branches when you see them. Since it blooms on old wood, or buds produced the previous year, only trim this shrub immediately after flowers fade if you need to control its size or shape so you don’t accidentally cut off next year’s flower buds. ‘Nikko Blue’ has mophead flower clusters that are blue in acid soil or pink in alkaline soil in midsummer to fall; grows in full sun to part shade, moist, well-drained acid soil; reaches 4 to 6 feet tall and wide; and is cold hardy in USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: Reasons to Get the Blues
content: Large blue hydrangea garden photo used to open the blues feature.

title: Good to Know
content: Most bigleaf hydrangeas, including ‘Nikko Blue’, bloom on buds formed the previous year. In zones 4 and 5, cold winters often damage the flower buds, so plants won’t bloom. However, Endless Summer® hydrangea blooms on old and new growth, so it is more likely to produce flowers in cold areas.

title: Reasons to Get the Blues
content: Blue hydrangea border photo showing a mass planting of bigleaf hydrangeas in bloom.

title: Laguna® Sky Blue lobelia
content: Lobelia erinus ‘Laguna Sky Blue’ is the perfect complement to tame a mixed planting of boisterous, vivid annuals. It trails like a waterfall over the edge of a container and can also be planted as a ground cover. Though more heat-tolerant than other lobelia cultivars, blooming will slow when night temperatures are over 70 degrees F. Shear plants back by a third, especially if they are getting leggy in the heat of summer. They’ll fill out when temps cool a bit and continue to bloom until frost.

title: Striped squill
content: Puschkinia scilloides var. libenotica is one of the first spring bulbs to bloom, with petite spikes of star-shaped flowers rising above clusters of strappy foliage. Each of the pale blue, almost white petals sports a dark blue stripe down the middle. Striped squill naturalizes easily, spreading by bulblets and by seed, so it is ideal to create a carpet of pastel color in early spring between newly emerging perennials and under deciduous shrubs.

title: Best Blue Flowers
content: Container photo and bulb close-up for Laguna Sky Blue lobelia and striped squill.

title: Broad-leaved grape hyacinth
content: Muscari latifolium gives you two blues for the price of one. Each bloom spike is covered with dozens of tiny, beadlike flowers; those at the top half are a light sky blue while the lower half are deep violet-blue. This grape hyacinth grows just a single broad leaf that curls around the bloom as it emerges. Foliage dies back in early summer, usually later than other spring bulbs. Broad-leaved grape hyacinth multiplies by bulblets and seed, so it naturalizes easily in a perennial bed or the lawn.

title: ‘Blue Jacket’ hyacinth
content: Hyacinthus orientalis ‘Blue Jacket’ provides a rich royal blue color that looks great in a mass planting or in combination with yellows, pinks or reds of other early spring-flowering shrubs and bulbs. Deer- and rabbit-resistant hyacinths are a good answer for gardeners with hungry wildlife because their strong, sweet scent helps repel animals that nibble on foliage or flowers of other spring bloomers. ‘Blue Jacket’ hyacinths make long-lasting cut flowers, filling up the room with their powerful fragrance, and they also make super candidates for forcing indoors in the winter over water, stones or in soil.

title: Blue pimpernel
content: Anagallis monellii is native to the Mediterranean region and is one of the few true blue flowers. Its brilliant royal blue petals are enhanced by a vibrant hot pink eye that almost glows, punctuated by bright yellow anthers. Blue pimpernel is low-growing and spreads quickly, perfect for hanging baskets, windowboxes and containers as well as rock gardens. It is drought tolerant but will bloom more consistently with regular moisture and full sun.

title: ‘Crystal Blue’ salvia
content: Salvia nemorosa ‘Crystal Blue’ stands apart with loads of sky blue blooms in spring to early summer. Pollinators and hummingbirds flock to the pastel spikes, but deer and rabbits will not be nearly as impressed. To extend the bloom time, deadhead the first flower stalks as they fade by cutting back to the next set of leaves where you can see secondary buds forming. In midsummer when blooms are spent and the plant is starting to flop, cut stems back to the base of the plant.

title: Arkansas bluestar
content: Amsonia hubrichtii shines in late spring with clouds of pale blue flower clusters, and in autumn its light green feathery foliage transforms to a glorious golden yellow that lights up the border. Arkansas bluestar loves the sun and tolerates dry soil. In too much shade, it can get leggy, but even in full sun it is a good idea to shear the plant back by a third right after flowers fade. This keeps the plant full and compact, but also prevents it from setting seed.

title: ‘Aurora Blue’ delphinium
content: Delphinium elatum ‘Aurora Blue’ mimics the brilliant blue of the sky and stands tall above many other perennials in the border. Bloom stalks can reach up to 4 feet. Plant it in a protected spot to prevent wind from toppling its floral towers. Despite its sturdy stems, it may need staking to keep the blooms upright. Once blooming is finished, cut flower stalks back to the base of the plant.

title: ‘Rooguchi’ clematis
content: Clematis hybrid ‘Rooguchi’ is not your typical open-flowered clematis. Instead, it is covered by an endless number of sweet, indigo blue to purple bell-shaped flowers that dangle from near-black stems. It will bloom all summer with no need to deadhead. Unlike other clematis, ‘Rooguchi’ doesn’t climb vertically; rather, it clambers over and through other plants. Since it blooms on new wood, you can cut all stems off 2 to 6 inches from the ground in late winter or early spring.

title: ‘Blue Horizon’ floss flower
content: Ageratum houstonianum ‘Blue Horizon’ lends subtle color and interesting texture that blends into any landscape. Powder blue-lavender tassel-like blossoms clustered atop long, sturdy stems make great cut flowers for bouquets. If you can’t find starter plants, try starting it indoors from seed 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost date. Though it will tolerate part shade, you’ll have better blooms on sturdier stems in full sun.

title: ‘Galaxy Blue’ lily of the Nile
content: Agapanthus hybrid ‘Galaxy Blue’ is hardy to USDA zone 6 and will die back to the ground in the colder regions of its range. A protective layer of straw mulch helps it survive freezing winter temps until it emerges again in spring. Globes of star-shaped, cobalt-blue flowers rise on long stems from a cluster of strappy basal leaves. It is a reliable rebloomer, so you’ll have flowers well into fall, longer than other hybrids.

title: ‘Victoria’ California lilac
content: Ceanothus hybrid ‘Victoria’ California lilac is an evergreen West Coast native that peaks in late spring with an impressive show of cobalt-blue flower clusters. Bees, butterflies and hummingbirds all flock to the scented blooms, but deer will leave it alone. It really does thrive on dry soil and neglect—you don’t need to prune or deadhead, but a quick trim after flowers fade will keep the plant tidy and shaped.

title: This or That: Hollyhock vs. Rose of Sharon
content: Hollyhocks are a mainstay of traditional cottage gardens and can reach 5 to 8 feet tall, with heart-shaped leaves and flowers that open from the bottom to the top of the stem. They need full sun and good drainage, and newer cultivars have been bred to bloom in year one and return for several seasons. Rust can be an issue, so space plants for air flow, water at the soil line and remove spent plants in fall.

title: This or That: Hollyhock vs. Rose of Sharon
content: Rose of Sharon, Hibiscus syriacus, steps in when spring-blooming shrubs fade. It usually blooms from early summer into autumn and is an upright, 3- to 12-foot-tall deciduous shrub. Compact cultivars make good subjects for containers, larger varieties can serve as a summer privacy hedge, and a single shrub works well as an accent in a mixed border. It grows in full sun to part shade and should be pruned in early spring if needed because flower buds form on new growth.

title: Asiatic Lilies
content: Summer borders get a whole new look when you grow the big trumpet-shaped, and often brightly colored, blooms of Asiatic lilies. Sitting on tall upright stems, they’re a sure way to grab attention early to midsummer. They bloom earlier than other groups of lilies and multiply faster too. Though each bulb produces just one stem, there are two to four buds on each one or more depending on the variety, creating a flower show that can last up to a month.

title: Asiatic Lilies
content: Grow bold-colored Asiatic lilies, such as ‘Forever Susan’ or ‘Heart Strings’, next to the patio to set a tropical and energetic mood that’s perfect for entertaining. Or try soft-toned ‘Easy Vanilla’ to create a relaxing vibe near a seating area. While most varieties have the traditional trumpet-shaped bloom that faces up or out, some varieties have more downward-facing flowers with unique backward curling, or recurved, petals.

title: Choose the Right Size
content: Most Asiatic lilies reach 3 to 4 feet tall. Grow them midborder to help bridge the gap between taller and smaller perennial companions. ‘Lollypop’, in the photo at right, is a bit smaller, 2 to 3 feet tall, so it’s more at home near the front. Pint-sized ‘Orange Pixie’ is even smaller, at just 12 to 18 inches tall, making it a bright addition to the garden’s edge or a full-sun container.

title: Choose the Right Size
content: At the other end of the spectrum, you’ll find some that grow up to 6 feet tall. Don’t think you have to relegate these beauties to the back of the border. Although ‘Karen North’ deserves a spot where you can enjoy its light fragrance, keep it away from high-traffic spots where its pollen can stain clothes. To prevent this, grow the lilies farther back from the path or choose varieties with upward-facing blooms.

title: Asiatic lily
content: Asiatic lily, Lilium spp. and hybrids, is a perennial bulb with pink, white, red, peach, orange, purple or yellow trumpet-shaped blooms in early to midsummer. It grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, has no serious pest issues, reaches 12 to 72 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Asiatic Lilies: ‘Lollypop’
content: ‘Lollypop’ has sturdy stems that don’t need staking. Each one is topped with three to four buds for a long-lasting show.

title: Try These Asiatic Lilies
content: Asiatic lilies are usually the result of complex crosses of several species and other hybrids. They’ve been bred for cut flower production for years, which is why you see so many varieties that have up- or outward-facing blooms at garden centers. Some online nurseries have a broader selection with more flower shapes; the photos here are just the beginning of what you’ll find. Be sure to check in with your local lily society too. Many have annual sales where you can find unusual varieties.

title: Try These Asiatic Lilies
content: These summer-blooming beauties are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8 and do best in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil.

title: ‘Iowa Rose’ Asiatic lily
content: ‘Iowa Rose’ is a Lilium hybrid with outward- to downward-facing rusty rose-pink blooms with a blush of yellow near the center. It grows 36 to 48 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide.

title: ‘Orange Pixie’ Asiatic lily
content: ‘Orange Pixie’ is a Lilium hybrid with upward-facing bright orange blooms. It grows 12 to 18 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide.

title: ‘Karen North’ Asiatic lily
content: ‘Karen North’ is a Lilium hybrid with downward-facing orange blooms with deep purple speckles and recurved petals. It has a light fragrance and grows 48 to 72 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide.

title: ‘Graffiti’ Asiatic lily

title: ‘Tinos’ Asiatic lily

title: ‘Elodie’ Asiatic lily
content: ‘Elodie’ is a Lilium hybrid with upward-facing double pale pink blooms and pollen-free flowers. It grows 36 to 48 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide.

title: ‘Secret Kiss’ Asiatic lily
content: ‘Secret Kiss’ is a Lilium hybrid with upward-facing deep purple, almost black blooms. It grows 36 to 48 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Great-looking lilies start with good bulbs like those in photo 2. Look for the biggest bulb you can get so that it takes off and blooms the first season. Small bulbs may not flower right away; they need time to build up energy.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Asiatic lilies grow from a concentric bulb, which means the scales are arranged in layers around a vertical stem, kind of like an onion. You can see in the photo at right how plants form roots above and below the bulb. The basal roots below the bulb help anchor the plant while stem roots above it help stabilize it and gather nutrients.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: Where to plant
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Asiatic lilies grow best in well-drained soil. Avoid spots with heavy clay because at worst, bulbs will rot, and at best, they may not multiply well. Full sun will give you the most flowers, but you can even tuck them into sunny pockets between tree canopies, where they can add a nice splash of color like the orange flowers in photo 3.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: When to plant
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: You can plant Asiatic lilies in spring or fall. Plant the ones you buy in nursery pots at the same level they are growing there. Bare-root bulbs are another matter: most gardeners plant them in fall a few weeks before the first hard frost. But Niels plants in spring because he’s found that the bulbs don’t root as well in his Washington garden’s wet winter soil.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: How to plant
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To plant bulbs, dig a hole three to four times the length of the bulb, about 4 to 6 inches deep, to encourage stem roots to form. This helps keep the bulb cool, so warmer soil temperatures encourage disease. Space bulbs 6 to 10 inches apart to allow room for good air circulation, which helps prevent foliar disease. Asiatic lilies are drought tolerant but need to be watered during dry spells the first year to help them get established. Adding an inch or two of organic mulch after you plant conserves moisture and prevents frost heave.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: To feed or not to feed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Feeding Asiatic lilies isn’t usually necessary. If the foliage is pale and lacking vigor, top dress around the stems with a shovelful of compost. Or sprinkle a slow-release plant food for bulbs or flowering perennials into the soil in spring. Don’t overfeed, though; too much food can cause fusarium rot.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: Deadheading how-to
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: As the flowers of Asiatic lilies fade, the petals fall off, leaving just a cluster of green seedpods. It’s a good idea to remove them to help the bulb conserve energy. Cut right below the seedpods, leaving as much foliage as possible to gather energy for next year’s show. Once the whole plant has turned yellow, you can cut the faded foliage back to the ground.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies
content: Annotated Asiatic lily bulb image showing stem roots, basal roots and the small offset that can become a blooming-size plant in 2 to 3 years.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies
content: Photo of healthy bare-root Asiatic lily bulbs in a wooden tray, used to illustrate buying firm bulbs without soft spots.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: Troubleshooting
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Unfortunately, deer and rabbits find lilies attractive too. Repellant sprays and fencing or caging are the best ways to keep them from eating stems and buds. Check out a few lily-specific problems you might encounter in Lily Troubles.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: Division helps
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: It’s easy to get more of the Asiatic lilies you love. In fact, this vigorous group tends to suffer from overcrowding more than other lily types. This results in less vigorous growth with fewer flowers. Divide clumps every 3 to 4 years to keep them growing strong.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: Dividing bulbs
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To divide, after the foliage has yellowed in late summer or fall, cut the stems down and use a garden fork to dig the bulbs out of the ground. You’ll find a mix of large, small and tiny bulbs all held together by soil and roots. Pull away large offsets, the bulbs that form right next to the mother bulb, and replant them 6 to 10 inches apart. Leave smaller ones, like the one in the photo above left, in place to grow a bit larger.

title: Grow Gorgeous Asiatic Lilies: Babying bulbils
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Because Asiatic lilies are so great at multiplying, you’ll probably find clusters of tiny bulbs attached to the stem above the mother bulb underground or just above soil level. These are bulbils. Asiatic lilies produce a lot of them. Grasslike foliage at the base of a lily stem lets you know they’ve formed. When you’re dividing the larger bulbs, go ahead and replant the small bulbils too. They’ll bloom in a few years. Sometimes you’ll also find tiny black bulbils growing along the stems at leaf joints. You can remove and plant these in nursery pots in late summer, but they’re more sensitive and take a bit more babying than bulbets to flower.

title: Lily Troubles: Scarlet lily leaf beetle
content: If you notice holes in the foliage and flowers, scarlet lily leaf beetle may be to blame. Adults are easy to see if you want to hand pick and drop them in soapy water. You can also spray leaves thoroughly with neem oil in early morning or late evening to avoid leaf burn. It’s most effective on eggs and the sluglike larvae.

title: Lily Troubles: Mosaic virus
content: Look for streaked flowers and distorted foliage caused by virus-infected aphids feeding on your plants. There’s no cure, so keep an eye out for symptoms early in the season and remove plants that are infected. Tiger lilies, L. lancifolium, are common targets of the virus. Grow this species at least 100 feet away from your other lilies to keep it from spreading.

title: Lily Troubles: Fusarium rot
content: This fungal disease causes the basal plate and roots to rot and is most common in USDA zones 8 and warmer. Above ground, the plant doesn’t bloom, foliage yellows early and growth is stunted. There’s no cure, and this fungus sticks around in the soil for years. So once fusarium rot shows up, don’t plant any bulbs in that area again. To help prevent it, fertilize only sparingly and make sure bulbs have good drainage.
