title: Astilbe
content: Astilbe is one of those go-to perennials that brings so much to the garden. Its distinctive blooms range from bright and bold to soothing pastels, and they last for weeks—even months when you have the right combination of astilbes. The ferny, pest- and disease-free foliage provides great texture for your shade garden, and deer and rabbits usually give it a pass. Astilbe can even grow in full sun if you have a spot with plenty of moisture.

title: Astilbe
content: Astilbe spp. and hybrids include Chinese astilbe, Japanese astilbe and star astilbe, with blooms in pink, white, red, peach, cream or lavender plumes from late spring to fall. They like moist, well-drained soil and can tolerate full sun to full shade. Keep them watered and they will reward you with long-lasting color in the shade garden.

title: Astilbe
content: Large shade-garden photo showing the astilbe border and the lush planting texture used on the opener spread.

title: Astilbe tip
content: For lots of these pretty plumes, water astilbe regularly or site it where the soil stays consistently moist. Then you can grow other moisture-loving companions, such as queen of the prairie.

title: Astilbe
content: Tall border photo of astilbe with the white caption box describing moisture-loving companions.

title: Grow Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Keeping your border filled with color can be a challenge, but when you grow astilbe it’s a snap. These beautiful blooms last 3 to 4 weeks, and when you grow a mix of astilbe with a range of bloom times, you can keep borders colorful for 2 to 3 months. Start the season in late spring with early bloomers, such as pale pink ‘Europa’ Japanese astilbe or medium pink ‘Flamingo’ star astilbe. After that, mid- to late-summer varieties like hybrid ‘Maggie Daley’ take over. The combination of upright flower stems, tidy mounds and deeply dissected leaves makes astilbe an excellent companion in almost any situation.

title: Grow Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Large astilbe border photo with pink plumes and layered shade plantings.

title: Caring for Astilbe
content: Water, water, water. Astilbe doesn’t do well with dry soil. When the roots dry out, the leaves get brown edges and can even die back to the ground. Grow plants in a spot that gets regular water or site them near a natural water feature. Is deadheading necessary? Some gardeners prefer to cut the blooms off once the color fades and enjoy the foliage as a ground cover for the rest of the season. Get more astilbe by division in spring when new growth is poking through the soil. Each section should have at least three growth points.

title: Brighten Shade
content: When you want to kick your shade garden design up a notch, astilbe is a great solution. ‘Red Sentinel’ and ‘Snowdrift’ both grow to about 2 feet tall and wide — big enough to make a statement but small enough that they still work well near the front of a border. You can see the wonderful contrast in texture between the lacy astilbe foliage and the broad hosta nearby. White flowers like those of ‘Snowdrift’ practically glow in deeper shade under the trees, drawing visitors along the path to explore more of the garden.

title: Brighten Shade
content: Astilbe border photo showing 'Red Sentinel' and 'Snowdrift' brightening a deeper shade planting.

title: More Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Astilbe’s range of flower colors and season-extending help are just the beginning of its versatility and charm. When you want colorful height for a border, you might not think about astilbe, as most grow in the 18- to 30-inch range. But there are a few taller varieties that make great border additions. ‘Superba’ Chinese astilbe can grow up to 4 feet tall and provides beautiful back-of-the-border interest. Looking for even more height? Try Appalachian false goat’s beard, which despite its common name is an astilbe native to North America.

title: More Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Large border photo showing taller astilbe varieties and companion plantings in a moist garden bed.

title: Astilbe bouquet tip
content: Cut a few astilbe blooms to enjoy in your summer bouquets. For the longest vase life, snip the stems when half to two-thirds of the individual flowers are open and get them in water right away.

title: Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: It doesn’t matter if you prefer the sweet crunch of a bell pepper or the fiery heat of a habanero; growing your own peppers is easy and rewarding. Sweet peppers have little to no heat and ripen through a range of colors, while hot peppers can run from the mildly spicy poblano to the five-alarm fire of a Carolina Reaper. Peppers are heat- and sun-loving vegetables that need a long growing season, so they are typically grown from seeds started indoors or purchased as transplants in late spring.

title: Scoville scale
content: The Scoville scale measures the hotness of a pepper in Scoville Heat Units. Capsaicin is the compound in peppers that produces a burning sensation. Knowing where a pepper ranks on the scale, from 0 for sweet bell peppers to 1,500,000+ for Carolina Reaper, helps you choose ones that are best for your heat tolerance.

title: Scoville scale
content: Scoville scale infographic showing heat levels from bell pepper to Carolina Reaper.

title: 4 Tips for Growing Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost date, using a heated mat if you have one and giving seedlings at least 16 hours of light each day. Transplant peppers after the last frost into full sun and fertile soil, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart and staking them at planting time. Peppers do best in a long growing season and will respond to consistent care.

title: 4 Tips for Growing Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Seed tray and transplanting photos showing peppers started indoors and moved to the garden.

title: 4 Tips for Growing Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Water peppers by checking the soil 2 inches down and keep them evenly moist to avoid blossom end rot. Mulch to reduce watering needs and fertilize every 2 to 3 weeks after planting with a liquid organic fish and seaweed fertilizer. Harvest sweet peppers at their mature size and color, clip ripe peppers with garden snips rather than yanking them, and preserve the surplus by dehydrating, pickling, freezing or turning them into hot sauce.

title: Be on the lookout
content: Blossom drop can come from overwatering, cool nights or daytime temperatures over 90 degrees F. Sunscald appears as white to brown papery patches when young fruit is suddenly exposed to the sun. Bacterial leaf spot causes leaf loss and stunted fruits; if it’s been a problem before, use resistant varieties, rotate crops and space plants for good air flow.

title: Meet 6 Types of Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Sweet peppers have little to no heat and a sweet, fruity flavor. Bell peppers are essential in the kitchen and the garden, while corno di Toro and banana peppers bring long, tapering fruit and plenty of versatility. Specialty cultivars such as ‘Candy Snax Mini Pepper Mixture’, ‘Majestic Red’, ‘Cornito Giallo’, ‘Carmen’, ‘Goddess’ and ‘Sweet Banana’ offer a range of colors, sizes and ripening times.

title: Chili Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Hot peppers can run from mildly spicy to fire-alarm fiery. Jalapeños are a kitchen staple, cayenne peppers are excellent dried for flakes and habaneros bring scorching heat and citrusy flavor for hot sauce and spicy salsas. Other notable selections include ‘Jedi’, ‘Fiesta Cayenne Blend’, ‘Red Flame’, ‘Red habanero’ and ‘Red Savina’. Hot peppers contain capsaicin, so wear gloves when slicing and dicing and wash your hands carefully when you’re done.

title: 1st Prize Foliage
content: Stacey Toomey’s 60×14-inch windowbox is attached to an east-facing window in part shade. An antique shutter on the front provides interest when the plants are still small. She bought three 12-inch preplanted hanging basket combos that included wing begonia, inch plant and potato vine, then filled in with individual 4-inch pots. Maintenance is simple: water, feed and trim.

title: 2023 Reader Container Challenge
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This is the time of year that containers are top of mind for every gardener. Half the fun of planting them is trying out new combinations or swapping plants out for new looks each season. The other half is seeing what other gardeners have come up with — a little inspiration can really get the creative juices flowing. Last year we put out a call to readers asking them to send in their best container designs so we can share them with everyone here. The response was amazing — our readers really know how to put together beautiful containers!

title: Containers that Make an Entrance
content: Shirley’s 17-inch-tall and 24-inch-square containers provide a brilliant greeting on either side of the sidewalk that leads to her front door. They’re packed with colorful annuals that bloom from spring to frost. The large-leaved coleus splashed with pink makes an eye-catching thriller, while globe amaranth and lantana are drought tolerant and don’t need deadheading. Shirley’s palette of bright, warm colors could easily be swapped for pastels or a monochromatic theme if that fits better with your garden’s style.

title: Sophisticated Color
content: Sandy’s container combination uses shades of purple to bring a relaxing vibe to her deck. Sunny yellow from the variegated vinca and bright magenta petunia adds some pop. Most of the plants are quite heat and drought tolerant and take summers in stride. To keep this container flowering, Sandy sprinkles Osmocote® on top of the potting mix at planting time, then fertilizes every 3 weeks with a liquid plant food.

title: Taste of the Tropics
content: Joyce put this grouping together with leftovers from other containers she’d planted up earlier, and it turned out great. Its bright and bold blooms from lantana and mandevilla bring warmth, excitement and a tropical feel to the patio. The plants don’t need any deadheading and are quite drought tolerant. Look for mandevilla varieties with a bushy habit, such as Sun Parasol® Original Red.

title: Keep Shade Colorful
content: A shady out-of-the-way corner can be a challenging place to put a container, but Claudia found a group of plants that thrive on neglect, providing color and texture from spring to frost. Snake plant, purple heart, tall sedum, lantana, asparagus fern and dichondra keep this sophisticated container going without much fuss.

title: One Terrific Trough
content: When you have a special planter like this 48×18-inch antique stone trough, you want to give it pride of place. Sophath has done that by incorporating it into the foundation planting so it sits outdoors in this zone 6 garden all year and the contents get swapped out seasonally to keep curb appeal high. Mounds of begonia, iresine and purple Swedish ivy cover the long stems of the row of elephant ears that provide lots of interest and drama.

title: Passionate About Purple
content: Charlene’s planter is really a plastic insert slipped into a decorative wrought-iron plant stand, but you can’t tell by looking at it. The growing conditions on the west side of the house in full sun can be harsh, but this group of plants did just fine. Angelface Blue angelonia makes a great thriller and provides a stately presence and loads of color from late spring to frost.

title: Cottage Garden in a Box
content: Linda has been trying different plants over the years to get a cottage garden look for the 8-foot-long windowbox just outside her dining room window. She finally discovered a combination that provides maximum color with minimal effort. This mix of annuals, from the upright angelonia to the bacopa spilling over the front, doesn’t need deadheading and looks great with just an occasional feeding and watering.

title: Flowers to the Max
author: Leanne James, CT
content: Adding a windowbox is a great way to integrate the storage shed in with the garden. Leanne plants 4 1/2-inch pots in a custom-made 36×10-inch wooden windowbox, adds a slow-release fertilizer at planting time and then starts using a water-soluble plant food every 10 days. Most of the plants are vigorous growers and need maintenance pruning every 3 weeks to keep the look full instead of wild.

title: Sun-Soaked Side Yard
content: Sure, your side yard might be hidden from sight, infrequently traveled or have minimal square footage — but is it sunny? With careful planning, this area can become its own secret garden: an intimate spot that delights all the senses with lovely sights, smells and even tastes. Take advantage of this full-sun situation and grow stunning blooms as well as flavorful edible plants. You just need to employ some tried-and-true small space design hacks to make it happen.

title: Seeing Diamonds / Double Duty Fig Tree
content: Purchase a customizable kit to make this diamond-patterned trellis of nylon line and train the clematis onto the wires as new growth emerges in spring. The small patio is a place to naturally stop and observe the garden more closely while you’re on your way to the backyard. Large, soft-lobed leaves and deep purple fruit of ‘Fignominal’ fig make an interesting focal point and it also keeps its leaves through winter, which makes it a great indoor houseplant for colder zones.

title: Minimal Effort, Maximum Benefits
author: Chloe Deike
content: You’ll want to get a start on this garden in late winter. It’s most economical to grow the annual plants from seed, especially the basil and the marigolds. Start a flat of each indoors 4 to 6 weeks before your average last frost date. When the seedlings have three or four sets of true leaves, pinch them back to the next lowest leaf node to encourage more branching and a fuller habit. When nighttime temperatures are consistently in the 50s, harden off the annuals and plant them in the ground.

title: Design Challenge key plants
content: The planting plan uses delphinium, marigold, Greek basil, bearded iris, balloon flower, tomato, blueberry, clematis, dwarf fig and two apple trees to create a sunny, highly productive side-yard planting. The design emphasizes a tall backbone of trellis and fruiting plants with lower annual color to keep the space layered and useful all season.

title: Tips for Growing Healthy Trees in Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Container-grown trees provide height in spots where you can’t plant in the ground and add drama and permanence where you might normally just grow annuals. Use a container at least 20 inches in diameter and height, avoid pots that narrow at the top and root prune every 2 to 3 years to encourage smaller feeder roots and prevent girdling. Many trees can be grown in pots for up to 20 years or more if the roots stay healthy.

title: Root pruning steps
content: Slice the bottom roots, shear the sides, untangle the roots and then replant the tree. Trim about 2 inches off the bottom of the root ball, shear 1 to 2 inches off the sidewalls, tease out tangled roots with your fingers or a hand rake and repot into the same container or one no more than 2 inches larger in diameter. Water thoroughly and keep the tree planted at the same level as before.

title: Alliums rising to the surface
author: Kristi Boone, MI
content: If you planted alliums several years ago and now they’re poking through the soil, it’s probably the winter freeze-thaw cycle. If the bulbs are completely above soil level, gently tuck them just below the surface. If only these alliums are affected, that is pretty normal. If your bulbs have been planted for years, as clumps multiply, young bulbs often rise to the surface. Alliums are related to onions and can adjust their depth to what they like better.

title: Q&A: Plant sale divisions
content: If you’re getting perennials ready for a plant sale, go big with large, robust divisions that have several growing points. Wash all of the soil from the roots so you don’t pass along weeds, insects or disease, label each plant clearly, be honest about aggressive growers, get newly potted plants established before the sale and check for patents before selling divisions.

title: Horticultural oils and pollinators
author: Hunter Reagan, AR
content: It all depends on time of day and time of year. Horticultural oils are intended to smother or suffocate crawling or stationary insects, so they must be applied directly to the pest. It is best to spray early or late in the growing season, while temperatures are cold and bees and other pollinators are dormant. If you apply oil sprays during the growing season, use a more diluted concentration and spray early in the morning or late in the evening when temperatures are cool but pests are still active.

title: Weed watch: Pilewort
content: Pilewort, Erechtites hieracifolia, is a native annual with tall stems topped by loose panicles that can look like buds that never open. Its tiny tubular flowers are held inside a tight bract, and after pollination the seedhead reveals tiny brown seeds attached to tufts of soft white hairs. It prefers moist soil in full sun to part shade and is easiest to control by pulling or mowing young plants before they set seed.

title: Colorful Shade
content: There are plenty of flowers and loads of gorgeous foliage in this combo to keep shade borders bright from spring until frost. Deadhead the hosta and coral bells by cutting the spent stems off below the foliage. The yellow corydalis and Solomon’s seal may reseed, but it’s easy to pull the ones you don’t want to keep.

title: One Tough Hosta With Long-Lasting Color
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When it comes to hostas you don’t want to miss, put ‘Wolverine’ at the top of your list. This fast-growing variety with blue-green leaves edged in gold has been tough as nails in shade or sun and looks good even with 4 to 6 hours of sun a day. Lavender flowers top the scapes in late summer, and the plant grows into a broad mounded habit that holds its own in a mixed border.

title: 6 Solutions Every Gardener Needs
content: Taking care of a garden requires many skills, and you might be a master of the basic ones. But for every gardener there are days when you walk outside and find your regular rhythm interrupted by an unexpected need. This bonus feature gathers six tricky situations so you can prepare yourself with the know-how to tackle them and be ready to keep yourself and your garden in tip-top shape.

title: Garden edge solutions
content: Use trenched edging to dig straight down 4 to 5 inches and create a slope that keeps soil in place. Brick or stone edging needs a shallow trench filled with sand, and metal edging can be pounded into place with a rubber mallet and secured with stakes.

title: Garden Solutions

title: A disorganized garden shed is slowing you down
content: Clear and easy access to your tools and supplies can make gardening much easier, and it helps you take better care of your gear. Separate tools and gear by size or purpose, use shelves for stakes and twine, keep a workspace for gloves and rags, and store long-handled tools upright by the door so you can grab them fast.

title: A disorganized garden shed is slowing you down
content: Garden shed photo showing tools, pots and supplies arranged in the workspace.

title: An aggressive plant is taking over
content: If a plant is dominating the border or reseeding where you don’t want it, remove it altogether. Pull out the plants growing in the wrong place, including the roots and stems if it spreads by runners. If it covers a large area, smother it with cardboard and thick mulch. If it’s spreading by seed, remove the flowers before they set seed.

title: The nectar feeder needs cleaning
content: A nectar feeder should be cleaned routinely, otherwise you risk harming the hummers. Drain the nectar, take apart the feeder and soak the pieces in warm water with vinegar. Scrub the basin and feeder holes, rinse thoroughly and let everything dry completely before refilling. Replace the nectar regularly, as often as once a day in hot full sun.

title: The nectar feeder needs cleaning
content: Photo of a hummingbird feeder used in the cleaning instructions.

title: Outdoor furniture is dirty and worn
content: A set of furniture that’s continually exposed to the elements can take a beating. Wicker should be dusted, washed with warm soapy water and protected from sun and moisture. Wood can be cleaned, dried and sanded; plastic can be scrubbed with soapy water and a little baking soda; metal can be wiped down with dish soap and dried completely to prevent rust.

title: Dress for success
content: Wear long sleeves and long pants, even in the heat of summer, to keep yourself protected from rashes and bugs. Hang a long-sleeved button-up shirt near your gardening gloves, keep a light pair of elastic-waist pants by the door and wear tall boots or long socks with your shoes and gloves to protect your ankles and wrists from potential hazards.

title: Your health is at risk
content: Gardening is good exercise and mentally stimulating, but there are also some serious hazards lurking out in the garden. Wearing the right clothes is a great example, and you can keep yourself safe and healthy by dressing in long sleeves, long pants, boots and gloves, then checking for ticks and using repellents when needed.

title: Mosquitoes, soil-borne bacteria and poison ivy
content: Mosquitoes can carry diseases such as West Nile virus, La Crosse virus and Eastern equine encephalitis, so remove standing water and use bug repellent to deter bites. Tetanus bacteria live in soil, dust and manure and can enter through cuts or wounds, so wear gloves and stay up to date on your vaccine. Poison ivy contains urushiol oil that can cause an itchy rash, so cover exposed skin, remove the vine carefully and wash clothing and skin after contact.

title: Chipmunks vs. Garden
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Did you know that a chipmunk tunnel can extend 2 to 3 feet deep underground and reach 20 to 30 feet in length, often leading to an extensive food cache? This story traces the discovery of a buried stash under a shed, the frantic replanting that followed and the ongoing battle to keep chipmunks from digging up newly planted beds. Even now, years later, the chipmunk or one of its relatives still tunnels through the garden just to let the gardener know who the real boss of the yard is.
